speechtext:
The House resumed, from August 19, 1987, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that amendments by the Senate to Bill C-18, an Act respecting National Transportation, be read the second time and concurred in.
Those are the two extremes. And as always, it is the middle road, the happy medium that should prevail.
[DOT] (MIO)
That is the position the Liberal Party has been vigorously defending. We said from the outset that we believed in a certain degree of deregulation. However, we feel that the kind of wholesale regulation the Conservative Government would impose on us would be a disaster for Canada in several respects. We think it would be particularly harmful to the
August 20, 1987

stability of Canada's transportation industry. In fact, whether we are talking about the railways, the trucking industry or air transport, our Canadian transportation industry is a going concern, it is profitable and creates and provides thousands of jobs for Canadians who are able to earn an honest living. We in the Liberal Party are still wondering why it should be necessary to overhaul completely an industry that on the whole is doing very well in this country. We do not deny that improvements and amendments to the Transportation Act are needed to keep up with the new developments and new competition that exist in this field as in so many others.
To completely overhaul everything and change the rules of the game through wholesale deregulation, as the Government intends to do, is a giant step that should not be taken. An exhaustive study of this Bill has been made. In fact, the Parliamentary Secretary for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Thacker) said yesterday in his speech that the Bill had received very careful consideration. The House Committee on Transport travelled across the country and heard testimony from people from all walks of life and every region in this country. The message we received almost everywhere was one of concern and of opposition to the Government's Bill. Only the big shipping companies are in favour of Bill C-18, and the Conservative Government is again abdicating its responsibility to act in the national interest, in order to act in the interests of a few big Canadian companies. It has become a fact of life that the Conservative Government is biased towards the wealthiest in our society. This Government works only for the big and the wealthy in this country when it is not working for those outside the country, and I am thinking of the multinational drug manufacturers who dictated Bill C-22 which we will be considering in a few days. It is crystal clear that once again, the Government legislates for the rich and the rich alone. The Government's insisting on wholesale deregulation of the transportation industry merely proves my point.
The number of companies that will be affected by deregulation is enormous. We will see an excessive concentration of our trucking and air transportation industry in the hands of the wealthiest exponents of those industries. That concentration is already taking place. And this while it was hoped there would be numerous airlines, each privately owned. We will still have many of the small airlines, but they will all be connected with one another and often belong to the same owner. What is even worse, it is to be feared that they will be under foreign ownership. Well, as Members of the Liberal Party, we oppose this across-the-board deregulation because we believe that the Bill is not a well-balanced one. We have no objection against partially deregulating the transportation industry in Canada to facilitate the shipping of our finished goods in Canada towards the United States and other countries of the world where we can compete with foreigners. The Government, however, has failed to seek the proper balance.
National Transportation Act, 1987
We are now considering a Government motion which accepts the amendments proposed by the Senate to Bill C-18. I can even quote part of a statement made yesterday by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise to speak to the amendments proposed by the Senate and to ehcourage Members of the House of Commons to concur in them. There has been very close consultation and the nine amendments will make a very great difference to the Bill and our constructive policy development for the nation.
I notice that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) is present in the House and it is rather interesting to realize that concerning Bill C-18, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport has accepted the amendments proposed by the Canadian Senate and feels that, quote:
-these amendments will make a very great difference to the Bill and our constructive policy development for the nation.
In other words, what the Government is prepared to do today is to recognize the legitimacy of the Senate and the absolutely essential role it can and should play to improve the various legislation which we adopt here in Parliament.
It is not the first time that the House of Commons accepts amendments from the Senate. What is rather particular and unique, however, is the stubbornness with which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs refuses some amendments from the Canadian Senate. That is exceptional. For throughout our history, session after session, Legislature after Legislature, the Canadian Senate has amended legislation adopted here in the House of Commons. With only a few exceptions, the House of Commons has always accepted them and always considered that the Senate had the same authority as the House of Commons concerning a Bill. Under the Constitution, both Chambers are equal. And the House of Commons and the Senate both have the right to adopt legislation and to accept Bills.
What the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs are trying to do is to convince the public that, by amending Bill C-22, the Senate has exceeded its rights and responsibilities. Nothing could be farther from the truth. All the legislation introduced in the House are later submitted to the Senate to be reviewed, amended if necessary, and returned to the House of Commons.
And as I am speaking to you, the situation can be summed up as follows: we are debating Bill C-18 as amended by the Senate which, as the Parliamentary Secretary himself put it, has done such a good job that all the amendments made by the Senators will be accepted. Double standards.
There can be only one explanation: the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is so obstinate as to reject the good amendments made by the Senate to his patents legislation.

This is not the first time this has happened. I will recall a whole series of amendments which were made by the Senate in the past and which were eventually accepted by the House of Commons.
I have here a study done by the Library of Parliament's Information and Reference Branch, and I did not ask them to go over to earlier centuries, just the past 25 years.
I have here a document that takes us back to the early 1960s. I am not referring to minor Bills, in fact the legislation we are Considering today, the Transport Act, is an important piece of legislation, yet it has been amended by the Senate and Government Members are prepared to accept them. Such was the situation in 1960 when a measure to amend the Income Tax Act came back here in July, 1960, with three Senate amendments. The House of Commons agreed to these amendments and Royal Assent was given on August 1, a full endorsement of the work done by the Senate.
The 1961 Act to Amend the Criminal Code in the case of capital murder was also amended by the Senate and later approved by the House of Commons.
In 1964-I shall not list all such measures because there are pages of them, but I shall simply mention a few to illustrate my point that it is quite natural for the Senate to amend Commons Bills occasionally, and that, in nearly all such cases, the amendments are accepted.
The Senate also proposed amendments to the Trans-Canada Airlines Bill, and these were accepted by the Canadian Parliament.
In 1966, an amendment to the Fund for Rural Economic Development Bill was proposed by the Senate and accepted by the House of Commons.
In 1969, the Pest Control Products Bill was also amended by the Senate, and after discussions, the House of Commons decided that the Senate amendment was unacceptable. What happened then? After consulting Government representatives, the Senate did not insist on having its amendment adopted, but did insist on the principle of this amendment and proposed a new amendment to replace the first one.
On May 14, 1969, the House of Commons accepted this new Senate amendment, which led to the Bill receiving Royal Assent in June.
This shows that, when people of good will work in close cooperation, there is always a way to come to an agreement.
I now come back to what is going on in the case of Bill C-22. If the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was less authoritarian, obstinate and determined to satisfy pharmaceutical multinationals, he could say that the amendments
proposed by the Senate to Bill C-22 do not meet fully the objectives of the Government, but that there might be a way to achieve a proper balance. The Senate could then, later on, propose new amendments which, as in the case of Bill C-157 in 1969, would be acceptable in the mind of the Government.
However, such is not the case. The Government is desperately trying to stir up a fight on the backs of the Senators and suggesting that the Senate is overstepping its authority by amending legislation. The Government should not really be so critical today, since the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport has himself accepted amendments from the Senate, as I have already pointed out which at least proves that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) is not as stubborn as the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.

I see that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who was listening just now, finds my comments rather hard to take and probably went behind the curtains to be able to breathe a little easier.
It is a fact that in all our Parliaments, the Senate has, from time to time, amended Bills originating from the House of Commons. The Ministers have always had the courtesy and tact to go and discuss the matter with the Senate and reach some appropriate compromise so that the legislation could be passed in the best interests of Canada and Canadians. Not like the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who wants it to be in the best interests of the drug multinationals.
I say that when there is a will, the House and the Senate can find a way.
I have some more precedents for Bills amended by the Senate and accepted by Parliament. In 1973, there was the Protection of Privacy Act that was amended by the Senate and subsequently approved by the House of Commons; the Act to amend the Northern Canada Power Commission Act; and the Statute Law (Status of Women) Amendment Act in 1975. The Senate proposed an amendment that the House of Commons subsequently accepted in June, 1975. There was also the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act that was approved after a certain number of amendments had been suggested by the Senate.
August 20, 1987

1 know about this, for I was then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. And 1 never felt my rights as a Minister had been infringed upon because the Canadian Senate had suggested a few amendments to the Bill I was debating before the House of Commons. Quite the contrary: In 1975, I understood and accepted these amendments proposed by the Senate because I knew that these amendments were improving my legislation. And I never felt that my role as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs had been debased. As a matter of fact, I was quite pleased to accept the sound pieces of advice of the Canadian Senate. I cannot understand why the current Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs feels his rights have been trampled on simply because the Canadian Senate wants to make a few suggestions in the best interests of Canadians.
The Petroleum Administration Act was another major legislation to which the Senate had also suggested amendments which were later accepted by the House of Commons. Of course, I could continue on and on. There were other similar instances in 1976, 1977 and 1978.
In 1981, there was the Act to amend the National Energy Board Act. If the former Liberal Government ever had a legislation at heart, it was the National Energy Board Act. Yet, on April 7, 1981, the Senate proposed six amendments to this Bill. The then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources did not make of them a life or death issue. He accepted these amendments from the Senate and the Bill received Royal Assent on December 18, 1981.
Well, since the Members of the Conservative Party came to power, they have been trying to pick a quarrel with the Senate, and they would like the Canadian people to believe that the Senators, because they are not elected, enjoy fewer rights and privileges than the elected Members of the House. Canadian judges are not elected either. However, we are not trying to imply that their decisions are less valuable and important because judges are not elected. In some American states, some judges are elected. There are functions in the judicial system that are elective. On the other hand, other positions in the judiciary are appointed. So, I have never heard that, because an American justice official in one case is elected and in another appointed, the one who is elected renders decisions that are better or more valuable to the American judiciary than the appointed one.
1 find false and unacceptable that argument by the Canadian Prime Minister and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who would have the people believe and imply that because Senators are not elected, their work is any less important and less valuable than that of the elected Members of the House of Commons. The fact is the Canadian Constitution gives that full and complete right both to Senators and Members of the House of Commons. And I am happy to state that the Senate did an excellent job on Bill C-18 and also Bill C-19, the other legislation that comes at the same time as Bill
National Transportation Act, 1987
C-18 and that would bring a major change in deregulation in Canada.
I would like to remind the House that Bill C-18 has been especially opposed because it is not definite enough as far as safety is concerned. It is incomplete, in particular for air safety, and in my opinion, it should have been amended by the Government at the committee stage.
I would like to quote some of the presentations we received from various organizations when this Bill was being considered. In particular-
-more specifically, the Canadian Union of Public Employees, Airline Division, which appeared before the Transport Committee on March 24, 1987. I would like to read an extract of its presentation which states:
A review of the American experience with airline deregulation revealed the following:
In relation to safety it states:
U.S. airline passenger safety has been compromised and jeopardized by deregulation. Airlines, in a competitive squeeze with low-cost opposition have slashed not only labour costs, but operations and maintenance costs as well. Spending on commercial aircraft maintenance declined by almost 18 per cent between 1980 and 1984. The average fleet age of commercial aircraft increased by almost 4 years during the same period of time.
Flying is becoming more hazardous in the U.S. as the effect of using equipment and personnel for longer hours with reduced maintenance is beginning to show. The safety buffer diminishes daily under the relentless economic pressures of deregulation.
In 1984, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration disciplined 16 of 43 carriers, including People's Express, Pilgrim Airlines and Alaska Airlines, after an in-depth inspection found major safety problems, including extensive use of unqualified pilots. Several carriers had their licences suspended.
Meanwhile, U.S. near-collisions in mid-air have jumped, and safety violations fines of commercial airlines are at a record high.
Near mid-airs (in-flight near-misses reported by pilots) escalated alarmingly from 311 in 1982 to 830 in 1986. Pan American, American and Eastern airlines were fined a total of $13 million for violating safety and maintenance standards.
Another of the dangers of U.S. deregulation is that it has brought hundreds of inexperienced pilots into the industry.
In at least 2 cases, that inexperience cost a planeload of passengers their lives, once right here in Canada. An American air safety expert said the Arrow Air crash at Gander that killed a planeload of U.S. servicemen in December 1985 was "clearly a deregulation crash. Without deregulation, that crew would not have been flying that aircraft under those conditions". ("Those conditions" included freezing rain-the same kind of weather we have to deal with here in Canada about five months a year.)
This was stated by the Canadian Union of Public Employees when they appeared before the Transport Committee. I think that their fear of having the same American experience in Canada is real. According to the people who know what they are talking about, deregulation in the United States is a frightening experience. Why would it not also be frightening in Canada?

August 20, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1987

I was especially frustrated by the attitude and the answers of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) to a question which I asked him Monday in the House. I asked what the Canadian Government was going to do to guarantee that tragedies such as the recent one in Detroit would not happen in Canada when the industry is deregulated.
The Deputy Prime Minister, a former Minister of Transport and himself sponsor of Bills C-18 and C-19 which will bring about this massive deregulation in Canada, rose and, affecting indignation, said that he found my question irresponsible. As shown on page 8118 of Hansard for August 17, 1987, the Deputy Prime Minister gave this reply:
I find the Hon. Member's question quite irresponsible-
I think that making that kind of allegation is totally uncalled for.
He concluded by saying:
For the Hon. Member to tie politics to a very serious tragedy is most
unfortunate indeed.
Mr. Speaker, Detroit was the scene of an appalling tragedy which took the lives of innocent passengers. As a matter of fact we have learned today that the accident may have been the result of human error on the part of the pilot. And what do we hear from spokesmen for unionized workers in the aviation industry: air safety has been compromised in the United States since the advent of deregulation.
I am not trying to score political points when I ask the Minister what he intends to do to protect Canadian air travellers when deregulation becomes a fact of life in this country. Everything seems to indicate that lower air safety standards are directly related to deregulation in the United States. Well, we do not want any compromise on safety in Canada and this is why 1 asked the question. My question was all the more justified that, in its January 12, 1987 American edition, Time headlined:

"Be careful out there. As air traffic soars, so does concern about safety in the skies".
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, 1 am not about to quote the whole article but I would suggest that the Deputy Prime Minister, former Minister of Transport and responsible for this Bill C-18, should read it and discover for himself to what extent the kind of deregulation which has been implemented in the United States and which he seeks to force on Canadians might play havoc with air safety in this country.
I am not the only one who is saying this. A number of expert witnesses who appeared before the Committee on Transport expressed similar concerns.

The Canadian Air Line Pilots Association also presented submissions on Bill C-18 to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Transport. They appeared before the committee on April 2, 1987 in Montreal. Here is what they said:
It should be unnecessary to point out that a profitable operation is necessary
for safety-
This was stated by the U.S. Senate in 1937 during debate on economic regulation of the fledgling U.S. transportation industry. It is equally true in Canada in 1985, 1986, and 1987.
The subject of airline safety appears in Bill C-18 at Clause 3(1 )(a) wherein it states that the objectives of the Act are most likely to be achieved in a free market system under conditions ensuring that the system meets "acceptable safety standards". We are appalled at the use of the term "acceptable" when clearly the public is entitled to and expects that the "highest safety standards" will be assured. Nowhere are there provisions which will assure that the highest level of safety, or even these so-called "acceptable" but undefined standards can be met.
The level of aviation safety in Canada is ostensibly the responsibility of the Minister of Transport who, through his Department, is charged with establishing certain standards and monitoring the industry to ensure compliance. However, in practice the level of safety we enjoy in Canada has been dependent upon air carriers' willingness and ability to operate to standards well above the minimum demanded by the Department of Transport, and on the efforts of dedicated individuals.
Of course, under deregulation the Department of Transport will continue to monitor and enforce the same minimum standards. But as efficiency and profit become all-important, the self-policing aspect of the industry will fade. Capital will be forced to trade as closely to the marginal line of safety as the enforcement agency will permit.
To quote from the Assistant Deputy Minister's keynote address at the Flight Safety Foundation's annual seminar in Vancouver on October 7, 1986: "-safety is not the end objective for companies-" In the same speech he noted that "-safety comes from the top and must be seen to come from the top". In their presentation, the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association said that it is certainly not seen to come from the top in Bill C-18.
The Liberal Opposition introduced an amendment at the committee stage. We tried to convince the Minister to change the words "acceptable safety standards" to the words "the highest level of safety". We were unsuccessful. The Minister did not want to budge. He felt that to do otherwise would be too constraining on the companies. It is a sad day when the Minister will not put safety ahead of everything else in terms of aviation. I very much regret that decision. We would have liked to see the legislation amended, as requested by the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association, but we had no success with the Minister.
It is the bread and butter and the security of the people who are directly involved in the airline industry, and they should
August 20, 1987

know what they are talking about. This is what they said to the Transport Committee:
Prior to deregulation in the U.S., many airline industry experts expected that as the economic regulation by the Civil Aeronautics Board disappeared it would be replaced by a higher level of safety regulation and inspection by the Federal Aviation Administration, particularly in view of the expected influx of new entrants. This did not happen. Rather, from an inspectorate of approximately 2,000 responsible for monitoring 237 air carriers in 1979, the FA A reduced its number of inspectors to some 1,300 responsible for 470 air carriers by early 1984.
Furthermore, between 1980 and 1985 much of the time of these inspectors was taken up with certifying new operators, so that the normal inspection process could not be followed. It was only last year that financial restrictions were lifted to allow hiring of additional inspectors, but the number is still, and will remain, below the 1979 level.
Since 1984, when growing safety concerns led to more vigilant and intense airline safety audits, we have seen record fines levied against numerous U.S. airlines, large and small, established and new entrants. Some have argued that these actions by the FAA have demonstrated a satisfactory level of inspection; we, however, take the less comforting view that there is clearly a very unsatisfactory level of compliance with regulations.
Experience in the United States since the beginning of the transition to economic deregulation has shown quite clearly that a greater burden falls to the safety regulator.
This is what the Nielsen task force was saying in 1985. Let us remember that that task force of the previous Deputy Prime Minister of Canada came out with those types of opinions. In other words, this is clearly the view of the Government. The Government is ready to believe and have faith in the industry policing itself.
It is true that for a number of years it has worked relatively well in Canada. Our record of safety is a good one. However, we will be working under a new environment. We will totally deregulate the airline industry with this legislation. Therefore, the situation and the circumstances will be different.
To continue to believe that we can let the industry police itself is dangerous. 1 believe that something must be done to ensure that government officials, independent people, will be able to check the work of each company in order to protect properly and effectively the public that uses airlines. To restrict it exclusively to the industry, as the Americans have done, is a very dangerous course to follow. We only have to look at what is taking place in the United States to realize that American authorities have made a mistake and are compromising safety in the air in the United States, because they do not have the proper number of people to do the necessary inspections. We do not want this to happen in Canada. We are begging the Government to hire the appropriate number of people in the Department of Transport and in the various agencies created to monitor the airline industry to ensure that safety is not compromised.
We have not yet seen evidence that the Government understands. We have not yet seen person-years assigned to the Ministry and the agencies to make us believe that the Government is ready to take its responsibility. We clearly believe that the Minister of Transport and the Deputy Prime
National Transportation Act, 1987
Minister are very eloquent in words but are very short in terms of putting money where their mouth is.
Let me continue citing the presentation of the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association before the Standing Committee on Transport last April. It reads:
Jerry Lederer, President-of the Flying Safety Foundation has stated: "Industry does not remain indifferent to tragedy, but it faces a selection of priorities based on limited resources ... When the highest priority is economic survival, then safety must take a back seat, and there is disturbing evidence that the traditional safety margins of the air transport industry are already being eroded.
As the representative of the airline pilot who is charged under the Aeronautics Act with direct authority over and responsibility for the safety of his passengers, crew and aircraft, CALPA is concerned at the insidious trend in the airline industry, world-wide, toward reduced safety margins.
Over the years, there has been a dramatic shift of onus in most areas of aviation safety. Where once it was safety first, cost second, with no questions asked, pilots are now increasingly faced with the burden of proving why a costsaving procedure is not safe, or the even more difficult task of showing why it is less safe to the degree that it should not be done. Where once there was a strong element of pride within the industry in providing the very best in safety and service, we are seeing more and more reliance upon the letter of the law. Cost considerations are gaining pre-eminence, as a financially hard-pressed industry simply has no incentive to spend more on safety than is required to meet minimum regulatory standards.

I firmly believe what pilots are telling us. Day in and day out these people have to live with what is going on in the United States since deregulation. We ought to listen when they warn us to be careful, and this is what 1 had in mind Monday when I directed my question to the Deputy Prime Minister. I reject the Deputy Prime Minister's allegation that I was indulging in petty politics when 1 asked him what his Government was prepared to do to make sure that Canadian air safety will not be jeopardized.
Allow me to continue quoting from this very important brief which was submitted to the Committee on Transport:

Nor is it only the commercial side of the industry that is being adversely affected. We also see it in publicly funded safety services, most recently in crash, fire and rescue services. All indications are that there is a general slippage in safety standards, an erosion in safety margins that could take as many years to restore as they have to deteriorate. If so, better alarmist now than apologetic later.
The challenge is to maintain Canada's traditional attitudes toward safety and ensure that economic pressures, which can only be intensified under deregulation, do not lead to lowered margins of safety. Anything "less safe" must be rejected; we are not interested in exploring the outer limits of the safety envelope.
Bill C-18 presents no provisions to allay our fears that the inevitable economic pressures already affecting all segments of the airline industry will also affect safety. No one other than members of CALPA through our constitutional objectives, has been charged with maintaining the highest standard of safety; instead there is a vague reference to "acceptable" levels. This shortcoming must be addressed.
Indeed, members of the Liberal Party have tried in committee to address it and present amendments to change the

August 20, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1987
legislation but without success. While the Bill provides something to deal with this, certainly Clause 3(1 )(a) was the place where we could have dealt with it. The Government refused to budge. Indeed, 1 have no hesitation in saying that the Minister is compromising safety.
Let no one think that CALPA is alone in its safety concerns. I want to say this because of the vicious response by the Minister of Transport to my questions last Monday. I was asking something that I thought was absolutely responsible. 1 wanted to know if the Government was going to take every possible step to prevent the occurrence of an incident like the one in Detroit. The Minister tried to imply that we wanted to make politics out of a tragedy. It was not making politics because what happened in the U.S. could certainly happen in Canada. What I was saying on Monday is what the CALPA people have been saying along with a number of experts in the U.S. Let me cite them. Canadian Aviation is an important publication and it said in September, 1985:
All airlines are cutting corners these days. Sure there are safeguards but the risks are being cut a little finer in the interests of the bottom line.
James E. Burnett, Chairman of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, said in 1985:
Under-capitalized carriers cannot afford to invest as much in training as the well-established carriers, so that there is less familiarity with equipment and procedures.
Here is what Larry Crawford, President of Avitas said in Airline Executive in 1985:
The current trend among airlines towards maintaining aircraft only to minimum FAA standards is disturbing.
Here is what Donald Engen. administrator of the FAA, was saying in Flight International in November, 1985:
We cannot accept any tendency for people to move down to the minimum standards. Deregulation in itself isn't bad . . . But this is not to say we have no problem for the future.
This is precisely what we in Canada are saying. Contrary to the NDP, which is vehemently and totally opposed to deregulation, and to the Conservatives, who want to jump right to it in a massive and urgent deregulation, we in the Liberal Party are saying, "Just a minute. Deregulation to a certain degree is not bad. Certainly it could be done. But let us do it in a way that will not compromise the safety of people flying. We will not compromise the employment of those who have for years worked in the industry. We will not compromise services to the regions which are accustomed to a service that will no longer be available if there is no ironclad protection in the legislation". That is what we are saying. This industry, if it is totally deregulated, will only go where it can make a buck. It will not continue to serve the remote areas of our country who have been accustomed to the services. Finally, let us not do it in a way that will compromise safety as happened in the U.S. and as will happen in Canada unless we have the proper safeguards.
I am not the only one speaking this way. I want to cite another important organization, the Brotherhood of Railway
and Airline Clerks who appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport when it visited Vancouver in March of this year. Here is what they had to say with regard to safety:
-a number of other facts have many U.S. air safety experts worried about the future:
The number of near misses have increased steadily over the last five years- from 311 in 1982 to 776 in 1985; in the first five months of 1986, 305 were recorded, an increase over the same period in 1985.
While the number of commercial flights has grown by 31 per cent, from 14.7 million in 1980 to 19.2 million in 1986, the number of air traffic controllers has declined by 13 per cent.
While the number of aircraft increased by 68 per cent between 1980 and 1984, the percentage of operating revenues spent on maintenance has declined from 8.9 per cent in 1980 to 7.6 per cent in 1984.
Although there has been a dramatic increase in both the number of flights and passengers, the number of FAA inspectors has declined by 33.8 per cent between 1979 and 1984.
These statistics were presented to the committee to indicate that this trend in the U.S. should not happen in Canada. They urged the committee to make recommendations to the Minister to improve safety and make sure the number of inspectors in the Department would be sufficient to do a proper job. What we have witnessed so far is lip-service by the Minister. There has been no clear-cut indication that there are going to be more employees to do the work effectively. In his report to the House of Commons for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1985, the Auditor General made the following remarks:
None of the Transport Canada regions was able to inspect all carriers in its jurisdiction at least once a year.
This is not a member of the Liberal Opposition speaking. This is the Auditor General of Canada. He is telling us that in 1985, under the Conservative Government, none of the Transport Canada regions were able to inspect all carriers in their jurisdiction at least once a year. The Government is going full steam with deregulation and it has not substantially increased the number of people to do the work. The Government is trying to pretend that it is not compromising safety. It is trying to pretend that the work will be done. When I asked the Minister a question in the House the other day-

Did the Minister know that the Department of Transport delegated-not: did the work itself-delegated authority to airline mechanical engineers to apply the standards it has laid down? I also asked the Minister whether it was normal to let the airline companies police themselves. The Minister answered:
-I find this question totally absurd from a Member who has had some experience in transportation ... I invite him to reread the Aeronautics Act and to reread some of the actions which have been taken by the Government.
1 reread the Aeronautics Act, but I have yet to see the Government's actions reflect it in the policies we need to implement the new legislation and ensure it will produce results. Until the Department or the agencies have the staff they need to do the work, these policies will be no more than wishful thinking on the part of the Government. We can

hardly ask the agency, any more than we can ask the Department, to work miracles with the number of person-years and resources the Department of Transport has been given. It can't. I repeat: If you are sincere and if you are honest when you say that you don't want to compromise air safety, more money will have to be spent. The appropriate administrative measures will have to be taken and the requisite support staff made available to do a satisfactory job, and not what your Department of Transport is about to do, which is to ask the companies to police themselves. That is what the Americans have done with their own airlines since deregulation, and the number of accidents or near misses in the United States has increased. I want to conclude with another quote from the CUPE Airline divisions.

The Safety aspect is of monumental concern to us. Examples across the border of horribly low safety standards abound and while the Government would not knowingly create safety hazards, they will happen unless there is a budget for more safety inspectors and the requisite number of firemen at airports and a regulatory body with teeth. This, in a nutshell, is the philosophy of the Liberal Party of Canada, now in the opposition. The number of firefighters at airports has decreased, while the Minister would have us believe that he has security at heart and takes steps to better protect the travelling public. It is clear that the number of inspectors and employees is not sufficient to meet the needs. On behalf of my Party, therefore, I repeat that we are deeply dissatisfied to see the Government move forward with this Bill which will result in the across-the-board deregulation of transportation in Canada. My only solace, before I resume my seat, is to say that to a certain extent, the

Senate at least has improved this legislation and we are greatful to its members for their contribution to Bill C-18.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak today on the motion before us on the amendments brought by the Senate but I cannot agree that small changes in spelling errors and French translation will really affect the basic principle of the Bill and provide the kind of transportation policy that Canada needs. We are very disappointed that many of the possible amendments that would have made the Bill a better one were not made and that the opportunity to do so was lost.
If there was ever a need for sober second thought, it was on this Bill. It is an issue of vital importance to all Canadians and, if I may say so, of particular importance to those of us in more remote and rural areas of Canada. It is an issue which affects everything from the price of a can of soup in my constituency to the export of car parts in other constituencies.
It is not an issue that is very exciting to many people and probably not even very exciting to the media. However, a Bill that throws out the chance of having a planned transportation system in favour of a market-directed game of chance has passed both Houses without substantive amendment, and the New Democratic Party says that that is a shame.
Deregulation conjures up very positive imagery. It has a nice ring to it: get the Government out of our hair, keep it off our backs, decrease bureaucracy and red tape. It appeals to the emotions of most Canadians. We must remember, however, that in the past, there was deregulation. Regulation came into being because deregulation was not working.
At second glance, deregulation as proposed in this legislation is, if I may use the analogy of one of our more sacred Canadian institutions, like a hockey game without a referee. The little guys will get beat up by the big guys and the people who paid to see the game will not see the game at all, but chaos.
Transportation and public policy related to it have gone hand in hand in developing Canada and uniting our vast land and have been the subject of many debates in this House. Transportation legislation then must be founded on a social and economic objective. In this case the social objective must be that of maintaining transportation services on an equitable basis for all parts of our country. Nowhere is the importance of this more clearly evident than in the north.
In Yukon, my home riding, a territory of some 200,000 square miles, we are accessed by one major highway and only one major Canadian airline since the amalgamation of PWA and CP. The cost of living in Yukon is at least 20 per cent to 50 per cent higher than in most parts of southern Canada. Much of the reason for this is the high cost of bringing goods to the territory, most of which are trucked in a minimum of 1,000 miles from the south.

August 20, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1987
Mining, which is a very large part of our economy, also relies heavily on good and economical transportation systems. A big issue in the Yukon recently was that a mine which was closed due to lower world market prices could only open again if economical transportation could be provided. I am suggesting that with deregulation such economical transportation would not have been provided and a number of people would have been put out of jobs because of that.
Our economy is as fragile as our climate. Temperatures range from 35 degrees above zero to 60 degrees below zero. Due to this, transportation routes are the subject of much conversation, speculation and often trepidation owing to floods, snow slides, and the very fact that we are so isolated. The highway is the lifeline of our territory and numerous jobs depend on it.
Parts of northern B.C. as well as Yukon rely on the major airline which goes to only two main communities. Therefore, smaller companies play an extremely important part in relaying goods and passengers between the smaller communities to facilitate mining explorations and to bring tourists to various sites. We are very reliant upon the small chartered companies and smaller airlines.
We know that transportation is expensive. For example, it costs more to go from Whitehorse, the capital city of Yukon, to Vancouver than it does to go from Toronto to Vancouver. It costs twice as much to go from Whitehorse in Yukon to Old Crow, our most northerly community. It costs twice as much to travel within the territory as it does to go outside. Therefore, transportation and the cost of it is frequently a subject of discussion.
The situation of Yukon is not unique in Canada. These characteristics are shared by rural communities throughout the country. Dependence on one major transportation system, high costs, unstable climatic conditions, long distances, and small populations characterize transportation systems in probably 80 per cent of the country. Efficient, economic transportation systems are essential to our survival.
The question before us is how best to achieve a fair system for all Canadians. The New Democratic Party does not oppose improvements to the transport regulatory system. We need less bureaucracy and red tape, better safety regulations and better inspections, but we do not believe that this legislation will significantly address this problem. This legislation is like the referee walking away from the hockey game and saying, "Go to it and we will see who survives".
We require common sense regulations supported by adequate funds for enforcement so that all parts of Canada can benefit from a fair and equitable transportation system.

Wholesale deregulation as proposed by this legislation does not do this. It does not take into account the geography and demographics of this country. Canada is not only Vancouver, Montreal, and St. John's, Newfoundland. It is Carmacks, Tuktoyaktuk, Cranbrook, Qu'Appelle, Wingham and many other small towns, not to mention Come-By-Chance. If this Bill goes through it certainly will be only by
chance that many smaller communities will receive reasonable transportation services.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
While rural areas do tend to have high transportation costs, at the moment we at least have a reasonable degree of service in many areas, speaking particularly of the north. Addressing air service specifically, fares are not currently subsidized by the taxpayer but, because of the test of public convenience and necessity, are paid for through averaging between high and low profitability areas.
Passengers in Toronto are perhaps paying a few dollars extra so that Canadians in less populated areas can pay more reasonable fares-not cheap, simply more reasonable. That is an example of what makes Canada a special country. Our public policies have been-not always and sometimes imperfectly-generally oriented to ensuring that there is some equity for the country.
We cannot be sure of what will happen under a deregulated system. Our system in Canada is very different from that in the United States where deregulation took place almost 10 years ago in the airline industry and seven years ago in the trucking industry. What is the verdict there?
In trucking the number of motor carriers doubled although the amount of freight stayed the same. Therefore, there are twice as many people scrambling to carve up the same pie. There was a 140 per cent increase in federal highway taxes. Insurance rates soared 200 per cent to 600 per cent. Trucking accidents increased 18 per cent in one year alone as drivers attempted to out-race competitors. It is estimated that since 1980 one-third of the trucking jobs in the United States were lost owing to deregulation.
In the airline industry serious concerns have been raised frequently about safety, working conditions for employees causing more stress for pilots and others, and poor route service in less profitable areas. The good news with regard to deregulation seems to be that larger centres receive somewhat less expensive services. The bad news is that smaller centres receive less service and pay more. That is the crunch for rural communities.
In order to give some background to the importance of this I will, if I may, refer again to my riding of Yukon, a place which emanates good sense in that the residents have elected both a territorial New Democratic Government and a federal New Democratic Member of Parliament.
I believe the situation in the Yukon illustrates some of the potential pitfalls in this legislation. In the Yukon there is a very fragile industrial economy characterized by high operating costs and relatively low volume. The majority of our trucking firms, for example, are small owner-operated family owned businesses. Compared to southern firms, even the larger firms are relatively small. The scenario envisaged under the proposal for deregulation could very easily lead to an economy dominated by large firms from southern Canada and potentially the United States. We share a border with Alaska, and what happens there very much affects what happens in the Yukon.
August 20, 1987

One might ask, what is the matter with this? At this point, local trucking firms are run by people who live in the Yukon. They are committed to the community, run the services in the community and even run for public office, participate in the little league and so on. They are there to stay.
Branch plant operations of trucking firms, if one can call it that, do not have this commitment. They are concerned with serving the high volume, high profit routes. Small firms will lose out. Those who are willing to provide a year-round service to rural communities will lose out because they will not be able to compete for the high volume and high profit routes.
We are particularly vulnerable in the Yukon in the summer, both through air transportation and trucking because the highest profitability is in the summer months, with tourism, mining and exploration and the transport of various goods. It is during the summer that heavy equipment and other materials can be transported. If the larger firms come in to skim off those good routes, the smaller, year-round companies will be left with the winter routes. They will not be able to survive because they must average out their profitability in the good months and winter months.
The Northern Aviation Transport Association recognized this problem and made a very impassioned plea to the committee, as did the Government of Yukon. They did receive a hearing from the committee about some of the problems these regulations would raise.
We will not have an equitable system under deregulation. The Minister may say that the problem has been addressed for the north by the inclusion of designated areas, under which my riding falls. This is quite true in the case of air carriers, but the main question for the people of Yukon is, what will happen now that we have lost the public convenience and necessity test? The Government has allowed the north the illusion of protection with its designated area, but without the committee and the appeal system of the Canadian Transport Commission, and without the public convenience and necessity test, how will the community complain about eroded service? Who will hear these complaints, and on what grounds can a successful argument be presented? What action can be taken if such an argument will be made?
As the House is well aware, my predecessor certainly has something to do with the Canadian Transport Commission. I assume that the Transport Commission is not being changed because my predecessor is the Chairman and will continue in that role, but certainly he does understand some of these issues, having been in the Yukon for many years.
Without the tried and true test of public convenience, the Government is creating great uncertainty for the people of
National Transportation Act, 1987
northern Canada with this new environment based on charging as much as the market will bear. Without a policy entrenched in this Bill, which clearly states that people come first, the Government is inviting every opportunist who understands our transportation problems to hold the north up for ransom.
An obvious question arising from the issue of the designated area is: Why did the Government stop with air travel? Surely it is not suggesting that truck transport to the north is less vulnerable, or that truck transport is not every bit as important? I am certain there are many areas in Canada which should have rail transportation protected under such a scheme as well, but neither House would adopt such a common-sense extension of the air designated area, nor would they make the air designated area effective. It is deeply disappointing and makes one wonder how earnest the Government is in wanting to protect the north from this policy.
I mentioned that in the Yukon we have a very fragile industrial economy, characterized by high operating costs and relatively low volume. 1 have also said that the trucking firms are small and owner operated. It is a very important character of our community that people can be facilitated to become independent and remain self-sufficient through the operation of their own business.
I believe that as this legislation comes into force we will see more and more problems. While we have been given some hope as to what will happen, we have not yet seen the evidence.
1 want to deviate somewhat from this subject, if 1 may, to say a few words about my constituency. We are fortunate in the Yukon because we have a population that, while small, includes aboriginal people whose ancestors have been in that land for over 30,000 years. We are able to benefit from that accumulated wisdom and knowledge as well as from the technology and science of other cultures. We are certainly fortunate in that respect.
In many ways, the Yukon is a microcosm of Canadian society and despite our small population, the dynamics of federal, provincial and territorial relations, of human rights and of immigration are readily seen and experienced.
I might add that in the Yukon, perhaps one of the most harsh areas of Canada, we have a number of refugees and immigrants who contribute significantly to the Yukon society and economy.
The impact of public policy in an area like this will be immediately and readily visible. Northerners are used to a struggle. The aboriginal people have a highly evolved culture and it is they who made it possible for Europeans who came to this country to survive. Today, they are struggling for a just land claims settlement.

August 20, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1987
In 1896, people seeking gold came over the Chilkoot Pass. One of my famous predecessors in the House of Commons, Martha Louise Black, was one of those who went over the Chilkoot Pass in 1896. In 1935, she became a Member of Parliament for the Yukon.
Despite the Yukon perhaps being somewhat isolated from the rest of Canada, it has certainly led the way in electing women, and now of course, in electing New Democrats.
The men and women of Yukon today, like their counterparts in the south, are really average working people who value independence and self-sufficiency. They value the lifestyle of the north and want to stay there even with the high cost of living and harsh living conditions.
We are concerned about the potential for loss of jobs through this legislation. Even the loss of a few jobs has an extremely significant impact on the economy. 1 think this is probably quite true in other areas of Canada as well, particularly in rural areas.
Deregulation does not meet the transport needs of this country. It will not further economic diversity. Canada's public policy has not historically been based on the survival of the fittest mentality, but rather to strengthen Canada from sea to sea to sea by encouraging a fair deal, not just for the many but for the few as well. I submit that this legislation will not do this. I urge the Government to implement a public policy that will be fair and equitable for all Canadians.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join with my colleagues in congratulating the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) for what was indeed a very fine speech. As one who some time ago had a large interest in this Bill, and spent a lot of time in committee when it was first introduced, going back to the White Paper, I must say that the Hon. Member for Yukon has summarized very eloquently and succinctly the problems which confront
those Canadians who live in the more far-flung reaches of the country, those people who are dependent in a very fundamental way on transportation services. Transportation services do not come at them in a flood of varieties but they are restricted usually to one or two basic services. The Hon. Member, 1 think, has done the House a service, having only been here a short while, in reflecting very well the concerns of her constituents.
Coming from Newfoundland, I share those concerns. I have to say as one who has been associate transport critic for some period of time, and who was in on the ground floor when the White Paper was released by the Minister initially, and as one who travelled the country with the committee listening to Canadians from across this land, that many voices out there were not saying that deregulation was of and by itself some kind of disaster for Canada. They were saying that while we need to reregulate, to make changes to our transportation system to help it be more competitive and able to evolve in changing conditions and times, we have to maintain at the same time some measure of ability on the part of Government and regulatory agencies to ensure the best interests of Canadians.
As one who has heard that kind of testimony given by quite sincere witnesses right across the country, people who crossed all political ideologies, I am amazed that today we have a Bill before us which came back to the House with nothing more than some housekeeping, house cleaning amendments. These are technical changes to ensure that the French and English sections correspond with each other in as exact a language as possible. These are minor changes.
In making those minor changes, what kind of substantive testimony by Canadians has been ignored? That has been done in a number of fundamental areas. This Bill would change the basic nature of what was formally known as the Canadian Transport Commission which is a regulatory agency that has operated at arm's length from government since the 1960s. It is an agency which is not a Liberal agency, nor a Tory agency, nor an NDP agency. It is a group of some of Canada's finest and most committed citizens appointed to act as the agents of the people of Canada, not of a particular political philosophy. The CTC is an agency which, in the past, functioned as an echo and voice for the people of Canada, including those who live in areas such as the north. Its mandate, in acting in that capacity, was to sensitize and recommend to the Government of Canada the kind of changes necessary from time to time in transportation policy to reflect the reality of this country. It is an independent agency.
That agency has been wiped out. It is gone with the stroke of a pen. It exists no more. There is a new concept incorporated in this Bill. Rather than being independent, autonomous, recommending transportation policy to the Minister honestly without fear of losing a job, and so on, this new agency will receive policy instructions from the Government of the day.
August 20, 1987

The Government of the day will draw the map. A Minister, a few Deputy Ministers and a few colleagues from Cabinet will sit in committee and will say what is the transportation plan for Canada. They will say: "This is the transportation map for Canada. We in our cloistered, hallowed halls surrounded by our chandeliers and stained-glass windows, walking upon our rich carpets, will decide here in this truly representative realistic House what those people in the Yukon, in Come-By-Chance and Baie Comeau need in transportation policy". They will take that map and give it to their new transportation agency which will make it happen. "Let us not let the reality of this country get in the way of our particular vision of what a transportation policy ought to be", is a philosophy which has never worked in our country of 25 million people, with a land mass as great as we have and with our diversity not only in economic activity but almost in cultures. It is almost ironic because just such a model could be found in the Politburo. It is the new five-year plan which will be issued to the transportation agency. If it does not work after five years, well, governments will change and a new philosophy will be heard and a new map will be given to the transportation agency.
Any hope of objective, independent continuity in the regulation of our transportation industries is lost in this Bill. That is not only a Liberal philosophy. It is not only a Liberal concern. It is a concern the committee heard from one end of this country to another. It was heard from people as diverse in their views as labour, business, town councils, chambers of commerce, and so on.
There is very serious flaw in this Bill. It is the question of foreign ownership. Yesterday we heard from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), who has really become the Minister of industrial affairs, the Minister of American industrial affairs, the Minister of American, pharmaceutical, industrial affairs, the Minister of multinational American, pharmaceutical, industrial affairs. He stands in the House and in an attempt to have Canadians swallow this bitter pharmaceutical patent Bill- "pill" Bill-he tells us that the reason we are all going to pay more for drugs is that we are going to establish and develop a brand new Canadian industry in pharmaceuticals.
That is what he told us. He told us that it was a priority of the Government, an obsession. We were told that the Bill was not designed in Washington, is not part of the free trade talks and that we are not caving in to the Americans.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Who says?

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I ask the Hon. Member, who pays his salary? Who pays my salary? Who pays the salaries of those who toe the line of the American multinationals? I do not particularly care who says what about pharmaceuticals when their salaries are being paid by anybody other than the people of Canada.
Having given us a lecture yesterday on the importance of Canadian ownership, the Government passes today a Bill on the transportation industry. One does not have to be a genius-one does not have to be an Einstein or even a Joey Smallwood, who was next to Einstein in his brilliance-to
National Transportation Act, 1987
understand that when there are 25 million in such a massive land, transportation is not a secondary concern. It is the way in which we move goods, people and engage in commerce with each other. It is critical.
But this Bill simply demands that all mergers and takeovers over $20 million and over 10 per cent of the voting shares of a Canadian transportation firm be reviewed by the Governor in Council. Anything below $20 million can just happen. In Canada, in particular Atlantic Canada, with respect to our trucking industry, for $20 million on any given day of the week one can monopolize that industry. It is not reviewable under the terms of this Bill.
Let us consider some of our other industries, for example, the airline industry and the shipping industry. When it is reviewable, what happens? It goes to the Cabinet of the day. And what is the philosophy of the Cabinet of today? It is that Canada is up for sale. This is the same Cabinet that believes that Dome ought to be purchased by an American energy giant, and just as quickly as possible. It is the same Cabinet that refuses to intervene in the sale of Dome to try to put together a Canadian solution, a Canadian package. That same Cabinet now provides us with a Bill concerning our transportation industries that has no means of ensuring an independent assessment or protection of Canadian ownership in this vital-
I would argue the most vital-industry that we have in Canada.
What is the rule south of the border? What rule do the Americans set for themselves, those who would now become, by invitation, the new owners of Canada's transportation industries? What rule do they set for themselves, those who believe in the spirit of free enterprise and competition, those who sit back in their ivory towers 25 floors up surrounded by concrete, glass and steel and smoking big cigars? What rule do they set for themselves as they personify free enterprise? I will tell Hon. Members what rule. They say that 75 per cent of their airline industry must be American-owned. When the United States of America, 10 times bigger than Canada and 10 times more economically powerful than Canada, says that it is necessary to have a rule that 75 per cent of its airline industry be American-owned, by law, we in Canada pass a Bill which sets forward the belief that there is no need for us to have similar provisions.
We Canadians, as legislators, as the custodians of those things that make this country Canada, have to ask ourselves whether or not we have done our job on Bill C-18. I submit that we have not.
With respect to regional development, I talked a moment ago about Canadians always bearing in mind what a large, diverse nation this is. Too few of us have ever travelled this country. We have been to Jamaica, Barbados and Europe. But too few of us have really travelled the width and breadth of Canada. Most of us who have travelled the country have done it on an airplane. It is but a four-hour ride. We cannot even really begin to comprehend how big the country is and how different are the interests of each of its parts.

August 20, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1987
The Bill before us was born out of a White Paper on transportation. When it was born, the 10 Canadian Premiers- Premiers of Liberal persuasion, Tory persuasion and NDP persuasion-met to consider their response to the Minister's proposal. There was only one thing that those Premiers from all 10 provinces, from all three Parties, could unanimously agree to, because some wanted regulation, some did not, some wanted more and some wanted less. But one thing those Premiers agreed to-one matter in which they were unanimous-was with respect to a clause being inserted in Bill C-18 that would ensure that the deregulation objectives of the national Government would not override the regional development objectives of any of the provinces. In other words, if in a particular part of Canada special transportation arrangements had to be made as a fact of life to move people or goods, then in that particular part of Canada these new rules on deregulation would not override the regional development objective. That is what all the Premiers agreed to. They asked that that principle be cast in stone, in law, in this Bill.
The Bill we have today merely has a statement acknowledging that transportation is a key ingredient of regional development objectives. It has no provision to ensure that the regional development policies of any particular province will not be overriden by the new powers contained in it.
For a Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who came to power developing and expounding the principle of his predecessor, the Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), that Canada was a community of communities, that there was to be no more confrontation, that co-operation would be the watchword of this new administration, I find it passing strange that this Bill, drafted in this place with its ivory towers, fails to recognize the particular transportation needs and the ability of provincial Governments to make special provisions in parts of this country that do not suffer from an over-abundance of competitive players wanting to provide transportation services. It is not there. 1 think that there are Members on all sides of the House who are not happy that it is not there.
I would now like to deal with safety. We have all heard over the last number of months about the increasing number of near misses in the United States over the last number of years. We have heard about the increasing number of near misses in air transportation in this country. We know that there have been a number of disasters over the last number of years, some of which are attributable, directly or indirectly, to deregulation, and some of which are still under investigation. What we know is this. Every single objective analysis that has been done
after nearly nine years of deregulation in the United States shows that safety has suffered.
What do we mean by safety? We mean training, maintenance, using aircraft and airplane parts and engines long beyond their normal lives because companies have been engaged in cut-throat competition. When one is engaged in cut-throat competition one has to save money somewhere. Contrary to what most Canadians realize, the most expensive part of flying an airplane is not taking off with a couple hundred passengers on board and landing somewhere else a few hours later. The most expensive part of an airline is training and maintenance. That is where the cuts have been made south of the border, and that is where the cuts will be made in Canada.
Last week the president of one of Canada's national airlines said that there was one airline too many in this country, so there will be a price war and one of them will have to go. When companies that are barely making money now, most of them not making money, engage in price wars, where will they make the price cuts? Cuts will not be made on the free booze that is given to passengers on the flight because that is visible. Cuts will be made on maintenance, training, and by deferring the life of an aircraft beyond its normal operating time.
This Bill does not deserve the support of the House. I hope that Members opposite will have the intestinal fortitude, the courage, and the vision to give it the boot it deserves. In Newfoundland we would say that we should pick it up by the slack of the pants and the scruff of the neck and fling it over the nearest wharf.

subsubtopic: WATER AND SEWAGE WORKS-ONTARIO LIFELINES PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in June the Ontario Government launched Lifelines, a program which will provide grants to municipalities for 33 per cent of the cost of repairs to water and sewage works.
When Ontario asked Ottawa to participate in Lifelines, it was turned down flat. At the same time the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) was announcing a $7.5 billion proposal for 10 nuclear submarines, a move questioned even by military experts.
Across the nation water and sewage treatment facilities are in need of repair. Every summer beaches are closed because of inadequate sewage services. Yet the federal Government cannot find even one thin dime, hiding behind the excuse of the deficit and the phoney argument that this is not within federal jurisdiction.

DANGERS POSED BY UNITED STATES NUCLEAR REACTOR

CANADA'S GROWTH RATE BEST OF MAJOR COUNTRIES
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity again to speak on Bill C-19, which we have discussed in the past along with Bill C-18. It is memorable that, after so much consultation and so much work by all the House committees involved, we have finally reached a consensus on the National Transportation Act, something which will be good for Canadians in general.
Time and again throughout this lengthy process, the Government has demonstrated the necessary flexibility to develop and modify the economic reforms mentioned in Bill C-19. Indeed, some amendments were made when the House standing committee examined the Bill last spring.
Without going further, I would like to congratulate the Standing Committee on Transport, its Chairman and all members of the committee from all sides of the House who worked so diligently with the provinces and all people concerned with our transportation system. We must remember that there are consumers, shippers and carriers involved in the transportation system and we have responded to the needs of those people.
The transition period during which economic regulation will be phased out was extended from three years to five years, that is, to January 1, 1993. The provinces have generally been relaxing economic controls on the industry for some time, so this gradual approach to change is already well under way.
The extension of the transition period will give truckers well over a decade to adjust to a less regulated environment. Some shippers feel that this is too long to wait. The Government, however, has also listened to the provinces and the trucking industry. A five-year transition represents a reasonable balance of opinions as well as a consensus among the provinces that will be implementing the reforms.
In response to uneasiness expressed by a few provinces concerning the final step to fitness only, Bill C-19 now includes a provision to study the effect of reform in the fourth year of the transition phase which will be 1991. The Government is confident that this study will not show serious problems, but if it does, the Governor in Council can extend the transition period.
When the Standing Senate Committee on Transport and Communications recently conducted its own independent review of the Bill, Senators felt that certain concerns were not adequately addressed in the Bill. Again, we were most cordial and conciliatory to these views, and in fact we recommended and accepted certain amendments that were proposed by the Senate.
I would like to take this opportunity to explain briefly these new amendments that will be brought forth in Bill C-19. First, the wording of Clause 8(5), paragraph (b), has been clarified
and now obliges provincial transport boards to have regard to any statement of public transportation policy issued by the Governor in Council after consultation by the Minister with the Government of each province affected thereby.
Second, a new subclause has been added to Clause 34 which requires the Minister to table a copy of the four-year review in each House of Parliament within 15 sitting days of his acceptance of the completed report.
Finally, a new Clause 35 has been added which essentially requires that a review similar to the four-year review be conducted at the end of each year from 1988 to 1993. These annual reviews must contain motor vehicle accident statistics as well as a progress report on the implementation of the National Safety Code. Again, the Minister will be obliged to table these reports in each House of Parliament.
As all Hon. Members can see, these amendments in no way detract from the essence of this Bill. Indeed, they enhance the measures that have been taken. Very close attention has been paid to the safe implementation of the economic reforms that Bill C-19 proposes.

Mr. Speaker, I believe at the same time that under Bill C-19 and Bill C-18-this is provided in those acts, those pieces of legislation-security is a high priority for this Government, for us, all Members in this House and also for other Canadian citizens.
Mr. Speaker, it is essential that in every Canadian transportation mode safety be guaranteed. And this is what we have included in those two Bills, Mr. Speaker.

For the trucking industry, the federal and provincial Governments and industry representatives have co-operated to produce a uniform National Safety Code. In March, the federal and provincial Governments reached an agreement on implementation and cost sharing, which was subsequently incorporated into the Bill. The code now has a concrete existence. All Governments are committed to implementing it. Key components will be in place in federal regulations when this Bill comes into force on January 1, 1988.
The Government of Canada has agreed to assist in funding development and implementation of the standard Canada-wide National Safety Code to a maximum of $23.5 million over the next five years. The National Safety Code will form the basis of safety regulations in the future. You know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker-

-whether we come from one of the 10 provinces, from the Northwest Territories, Newfoundland, western Canada, British Columbia, or the northern part of the Northwest Territories and Yukon, it is important for us to have a safety code for our transportation system in Canada.
August 20, 1987



Several key elements of the code will be included in the federal safety regulations. The detailed standards for these regulations will be finalized by the end of this month. Hence, once this Bill is passed, federal regulations setting out safety requirements for both trucks and buses will be in place well before the move from reverse onus to fitness only in January of 1993.
Furthermore, Parliament will be provided with a mechanism for knowing what is going on in the key areas of extraprovincial motor vehicle safety and highway accidents. While available evidence indicates that there is no causal link between economic regulatory reform and safety, many believe there is a connection. The preparation of these reports will dispel any fears that the Parliament of Canada is proceeding with economic regulatory reform of this important transportation industry without first putting in place a mechanism which will enable it to monitor the situation over the next few years.
This should not be misconstrued to mean that we have no highway safety at this time. Canada has an excellent safety record but we are determined to improve it. We already have a fine regime of safety regulations in each of the provinces and territories. Indeed, a number of the elements of the new safety code are already in place in one or more provinces. There will be improvements made to the safety standards in provincial regulations, some of which will be ready by January of 1988 and the remainder of which will be ready by mid-1989.
The provinces have made a commitment in consultation with the federal Government, with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and especially with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to have enforcement resources in place by the end of 1989 in order to police these improvements. The improvements that will exist in the new safety code and Bill C-19 include, first, a safety requirement for obtaining an operating licence. For the first time in legislation, all applicants for extraprovincial trucking licences will have to meet tough safety standards. Second, we will have uniform safety requirements for all extra-provincial traffic among the provinces. In the past we have had different codes and different regulations in each province. We are bringing all of Canada together. Third, we will have a national enforcement scheme based on company and individual driver safety deficiency records which will be available to all provinces. Fourth, we will have annual reports tabled in both Houses of Parliament reporting on trends in extra-provincial motor vehicle accidents and on progress in implementing rules and standards governing the safe operation of extra-provincial undertakings.
Economic regulatory reform includes the most effective enforcement tool, the linking of safety compliance with an operating licence. Furthermore, implementation of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act on January 1, 1988, will maintain pressure on the provinces to meet the implementation forecast for the safety code.
Bills C-18 and C-19 are of the utmost importance to our country. We began creating them, not in the last two or three
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
weeks but over a number of years. It has taken in excess of 20 years to revamp our National Transportation Act.
I speak as the representative of my riding, Bonaventure- Iles-de-la-Madeleine, but also for all Canadians when I say that due to the Canadian geography we must create a system of transportation for the shippers, carriers and consumers that is reliable. Regardless of what the Opposition says, safety will never be compromised. We cannot use isolated examples of what has happened in Africa, Europe or the United States. Millions of Canadians have travelled on our highways, our trains and our airplanes. We have an impeccable record.
The Opposition may say that this legislation is bad but, Mr. Speaker, it is good. As the Vice-Chairman of the Transport Committee, as a Member of Parliament, and as a Canadian, I sincerely believe that Bill C-18 dealing with our trucking industry and Bill C-19 dealing with economic regulatory reform will be good.
The Government has attempted to develop a balanced package of reforms which removes obstacles to the growth of our economy and trade with the rest of the world. Over-all, I believe that Bills C-19 and C-18 represent a balance for all concerned; our shippers and carriers and their employees, consumers, air travellers and others in every region of Canada.
