Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in the debate on the motion to support the amendments that were sent to us by the Senate. Once more, amendments made by the Canadian Senate to a Bill have been found in order by the Government. I commend the Hon. Member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Gray) for accepting on behalf of the Government, on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) those amendments from the Canadian Senate.
It is therefore clear that the Canadian Senate, which has a role to play in the same way as the House of Commons in discussing and accepting or proposing provisions to a Bill, is doing its work. In this instance, the Senate found it useful and worthwhile to improve Bill C-19, and this is why we support the motion to accept the amendments made by the Canadian Senate in the area of trucking by extra-provincial firms. I can say immediately that we accept these amendments. We find it quite appropriate for the Canadian Senate to propose occasionally amendments to legislation which was first considered in the House of Commons. I can only repeat how sorry I am that the flexibility shown by the Minister of Transport in accepting the amendments proposed by the Senate to the Bills sponsored by himself or his Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Thacker) is not shared by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre). I do not understand why one Minister would find amendments from the Senate acceptable while another says that the Senate is overstepping its authority by proposing amendments to Bill C-22. What is good for Bill C-19 could be just as good for Bill C-22, and I find it strange that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs would refuse to consider such amendments.

August 20, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
In any event, I would like to say that, on the substance of this Bill, the Liberal Party of Canada has been critical right from the start because we believe that the Conservative Government, inspired by a free competition theory which has serious weaknesses, and inspired even more by its desire to reduce the costs of the Canadian transport system, is now destroying the regulatory basis of the Canadian trucking industry.
Basically, the Conservative philosophy seems to be that the Canadian transport industry should catch up with the deregulation which has already taken place in the United States. Unfortunately, the Conservative position on transport deregulation virtually ignores the harmful effects of American-type deregulation on the Canadian trucking industry, and most important, the transport cost increases which will fall on Canadian manufacturers, who will thus lose some of their competitivity on the market as they will have to transfer these higher costs to consumers.
The Canadian Trucking Association states in its presentation to the Standing Committee on Transport that deregulation has clearly contributed in the United States to an increase in competition and shipping costs and to a decrease in productivity, reflecting a deterioration of the financial position of the trucking industry and an increase in the cost of transporting goods.
If there is one thing that the deregulation of the trucking industry in the United States has taught us, it is that there can be no compensatory rates on the basis of service in the trucking industry. On the one hand, we have seen a proliferation of full-load carriers, and on the other, a strong concentration of large, long-haul carriers. The losers are the regional and inter-regional carriers who have mixed loads and provide long distance services.
Moreover, the trucking industry is not alone to suffer from deregulation in the United States. Smaller manufacturing businesses unable to ship large quantities over long distances, which would allow them to benefit from the discounts offered by the carriers, must pay higher prices to compensate the lower rate given to those who ship goods in large quantities.
As we can see, the principle that large shippers pay less and small shippers pay more has serious consequences on all businesses, and not only on carriers already established in Canada. It is quite possible that deregulation in Canada will remove the value of operating licenses in financial statements. As many Canadian carriers use the value of their license as security for credit from the banks, the value of their business will disappear with that of their operating license. All Canadian trucking firms will find it ever more difficult to borrow money and, without Government assistance, they will not be able to compete successfully with the major American carriers.
Unlike the Conservative Government, the Liberal Party is not in favour of deregulating the trucking industry. We said so when the White Paper entitled Freedom to Move was tabled,
we said the same thing when Bill C-19 came up for second reading here in the House and when is was scrutinized by the Committee on Transport, a parliamentary committee of the House of Commons which heard representations from various groups and people interested in trucking in Canada. We repeated the same thing at the time that, if the Conservative Government was really intent on seeing this deregulation project through, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had to take the opportunity of his Budget presentation to do something to help trucking firms be at least on an equal footing with the major American carriers to be in a position to compete with them.
Sad to say, the Minister of Finance unveiled his tax reform, but he did not say a word about this very important question of the support he might have given Canadian truckers. Indeed, American truckers are way ahead in their country if we compare them with our trucking firms and the tax situation they are faced with here in Canada.
We in the Liberal Party recommended introducing a compensation mechanism in the form of a tax rebate for the trucking industry, so that shippers would be compensated for the drop in value of an operating licence issued under current rules of access.
When a company is not in good shape and is near bankruptcy, this artificial value diminishes and the guarantee ceases to exist. When this happens, the banks, as we know very well, call in their loans. If the companies were compensated in the form of a kind of tax relief that would correspond to this depreciation of their assests, Canadian shippers could at least survive. Unfortunately, the Minister of Finance failed to take this into consideration. Today, now that we have reached the last stage in adopting Bill C-19, it is clear the U.S. trucking companies will have an unfair advantage when they come to compete with Canadian companies.
Deregulating the trucking industry means that we are opening the door to American trucking companies who will come here and take a lucrative market away from Canadian companies. They already have tax benefits. They pay a lot less for their gas in the United States than we do in Canada, and in many cases, wages and working conditions in the United States are less attractive than in Canada. We have always wondered why the Conservative Government insisted on dismantling a system that, on the whole, has provided stable employment in the trucking industry in Canada, and why it wanted to get rid of something that is working quite well in this country. We have a competitive trucking industry that meets Canada's needs and the needs of all Canadians. Thousands of workers earn a decent living in our trucking industry. To satisfy certain specific economic interests of big shippers, and for the sake of deregulation at any cost, the Conservative Government is about to seriously undermine a prosperous Canadian industry to promote competition that will
August 20, 1987

come almost exclusively from big trucking companies in the United States. We find this most unfortunate.
But there is more. In addition to the threat that Canadian trucking companies will be swallowed up by U.S. companies, there is also the highway safety factor.
[DOT]	(1530)

Transportation is different from most commercial activity. A fundamental difference dictating reaction to commercial forces is that the product, which in this case is a service, has no shelf life whatsoever. If a trucker has a load from point A to point B, and he has to get back to point A, absorbing costs associated with that return move, he can be persuaded under hyper-competitive conditions to back-haul traffic at an extremely depressed rate to cover his out of pocket expenses. That is a sensible market decision for the mode.
It has inevitable long term consequences, as one can imagine. Multiply that by thousands of truckers, all competing to some extent in each other's market-places, with one's man head-haul being another man's back-haul, and there is a potential for destructive competition, at least until a massive shake-up spends itself.
Therein lies the connection to highway safety. The independent trucker, in particular, faced with payments on his rig, expensive maintenance bills, or that atrocious insurance premium, has no alternative if he is to survive in the short term but to ignore hours of service restrictions if he can find another load, or defer maintenance as long as his truck will move. It is these attributes of hyper-competition that result in a deteriorating safety record in association with deregulation, in the absence of an effective and adequately enforced safety regime.
This is exactly what took place in the United States. It has become very clear that after some years of deregulation of the trucking industry in the United States, this phenomenom has now become a very serious problem there.
We in the Liberal Party who have been discussing this Bill have told the Government to be careful, to examine the experiment in the United States and to ensure that what is happening there will not happen in Canada. In doing that, we did not take it out of our minds. It was not done in abstraction.
[DOT]	(1540)
We have looked at the experiment in the United States. We have studied it and have listened to some experts who have written on the subject. I would like to quote Mr. Nicholas Glaskowsky who wrote a very important essay entitled "Effects of Deregulation on Motor Carriers". This essay has been prepared for the ENO Foundation in the United States. We should take a very close look at what he said because I think it is certainly important, on the eve of deregulating the trucking industry in Canada, to see whether or not it was a
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
useful and appropriate experiment in the United States. Mr. Glaskowsky states:
Depending on the model, a new over-the-road tractor today costs about $80,000, give or take a few thousand. That is a lot of money. A dozen of them-with a few spare tires thrown in-cost about a million dollars. A motor carrier strapped for cash in an intensely competitive deregulated environment has got to consider alternatives to equipment replacement. The only realistic alternative is to keep and operate the equipment longer before replacing it.
The necessary concomitant to using older tractors and trailers is that they need more maintenance. But, maintenance costs money. And, worse from the standpoint of safety, some types of maintenance can be deferred. In fact, a great deal of maintenance can be deferred, the only limitation being a nonfunctioning item that literally prevents the vehicle from being driven.
After five years of deregulation three trends are fairly clear: (1) the equipment fleet of the motor carrier industry is aging, (2) a lot of maintenance (expense) is being deferred, and (3) the motor carrier accident rate is increasing.
Part of the cause of the increasing accident rate is probably due to the use of many more less experienced drivers by new entrants and non-union firms. The cause and effect relationship between good and poor drivers on the one hand, and properly and improperly maintained equipment on the other, is fuzzy, but clearly exists. For example, an experienced and careful driver may be able to handle a tractor-trailer with brakes he has "taken up," if he "takes it easy," whereas a poor and/or inexperienced driver would stand a good chance of having an accident if he drove that same rig.
There is no question but that the motor carrier equipment fleet is aging. There is also no question as to the cause of this. It is lack of money for the purchase of new equipment.
I am sorry?

I thank Hon. Members for allowing me to complete my remarks. 1 will not abuse their good disposition and will speed up my remarks.
I was citing Mr. Glaskowsky who was describing the situation in the United States. 1 will continue:
There is no reason to believe that this trend will lessen in the foreseeable future. Indeed, there is every rational reason to believe that it will continue and may even get worse.
Maintenance, especially preventive maintenance, can do much to keep older equipment safely in use. Carried to an extreme, it probably can overcome all or nearly all of the safety concerns involved. But, such a maintenance-practice extreme is also extremely costly. And that's the problem. The cost/profit squeeze brought about by deregulation affects mostly those carriers who can afford it the least in regard to aging equipment and the associated need for greater maintenance expense. One state (California) attributes an increase in its accident rate to the safety related effects of deregulation.
What is happening in the United States will inevitably happen in Canada. It is true that California, after the deregulation of its trucking industry, has decided to reregulate because of the level of accidents. It is interesting to note what is happening in California. Based on its experience with complete state deregulation, complementing its regulations, they are now deciding to redeem the situation by reintroducing a form of rate regulation. 1 hope we will not have to go through this terrible process in Canada, to deregulate, to destabilize the Canadian trucking industry, to create a number of accidents on the road and the loss of good jobs for Canadian workers to the detriment of American workers, because quite clearly, what will happen, as has been predicted by the industry, is that there will be excessive concentration of the trucking industry in Canada. Every time there is concentration of ownership, there are mergers of firms. The very first people who are affected by these mergers are the workers, employees of these companies who are losing their jobs. The process is always the same. One merges two companies and then one tries to streamline the operation and improve the efficiency and productivity of the two new companies. In the process, inevitably there are a number of employees who lose their jobs. We will see this happening in the trucking industry in Canada.
More important, the Canadian trucking industry has told us that what will happen is that it will not be able to sustain the competition of some major American trucking companies and will lose some of its market, some of its more productive and financially viable routes. This is a danger which is very real. I think deregulation in Canada will create this situation. If the Conservative Government goes ahead irrespective of the advice it is receiving, we will then be forced to do like the Californian people and reregulate after a bad experiment.
We have been saying all along that we should not do it. Let us put the proper safeguards in the legislation in order to ensure that we are doing it right. If we are able to take advantage of the experience of others, let us take it, and let us do it right in Canada in the first place. Both the Canadian Trucking Association and the Ontario Trucking Association have made representation to the Canadian Government to implement the deregulation process the right way.
One matter which has been outlined to the Government and which it has not been taking care of, something which I regret very much, is with respect to the safety gap that exists in Bill C-19. A balkanized approach to safety has developed. This has created an extremely dangerous situation. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has indicated that the national safety code is to be phased in between 1988 and 1990. Moreover, the Minister of Transport has stated that the main elements of the national safety code will be in place by January 1, 1989.
For the period between January 1, 1988, which is the proposed date of the regulatory change, and January 1, 1989, there will be inadequate safeguards to irresponsible and unsafe trucking operations. This is quite clear. The deficiency there is important and should have been addressed by Ministers but it was literally refused every time we brought it to their attention.

The Quebec Trucking Association also made representations on Bill C-19. I would like to briefly quote from them.
"Let us now review the situation. The Government wants to deregulate on January 1, 1988; yet there is no indication that we would have in place a standardized road safety code throughout Canada before 1990 or even 1991.
"Each province interprets in its own way its role in that area, and there is no central leadership other than a pious wish to arrive at a uniform code some day in the future.
"Imagine what could happen if anyone can enter trucking without any ability and qualification tests, without rules and without any regulatory process to protect the public interest, on matters of vehicle safety for instance.
"What we cannot understand is why this Government wants at all costs to travel a road the Americans already are starting to steer away from. Looking at what is going on in United States under deregulation, we find it led to increased road accidents, increased bankruptcies, concentration in the hands of a few large corporations that conquered new markets through price discrimination and unfair practices."
We share the same view exactly. We believe that this measure to deregulate trucking in Canada has been put together hastily. Without the required mechanism for adequate safety, we cannot understand that this Government wants to deregulate trucking immediately without at the same time putting in place a national road safety code.
Each time we have asked the Minister of Transport whether he could guarantee that a highway safety code will be implemented throughout Canada, he has told us that he has received the assurance that the provinces will co-operate. However, he has never been able to give us a clear and specific commitment that a uniform national code will be implemented in all the provinces. We are therefore about to deregulate the trucking industry with no proper guarantees.
August 20, 1987

We are about to deregulate our trucking industry in exactly the same way as the Americans did, without proper guarantees, and I must say that we are running the same risks as in the United States of disastrous consequences because of an increased number of highway accidents caused by massive deregulation. I have no hesitation in saying that, because of the indifference of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), we shall have the same problems on Canadian highways in a few months or years because of this massive, ill-prepared and ill-orchestrated deregulation imposed by the Conservative Government.

Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to listen to the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) talk about deregulation. He does a very effective job of explaining his position and all the ills that go along with deregulation. As 1 said in an earlier debate, it is interesting to hear a former Liberal cabinet Minister take that line since it was his seatmate, a former Minister of Transport, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), who was really the father of deregulation in Canada. He started us down the road, the track, the flight path of deregulation. There is no question that that is the case.
It is interesting to see that members of the Liberal Party when in opposition combine with the New Democrats to fight such legislation, legislation which I suspect they would have introduced were they the Government today. It reminds me of another piece of legislation, one which we will probably be dealing with tomorrow. Bill C-22. A former Liberal Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Judy Erola, was looking at legislation very similar to what the Conservatives have brought forward with respect to changing the Patent Act as far as it affects generic drugs. Ms. Erola is now the chief spokesperson for the large American-based pharmaceutical companies in Canada. She is their chief lobbyist and was speaking on their behalf on The Journal last night. It is interesting to hear how the Liberals say one thing when in opposition and yet the very actions they take when in government are similar to the actions now being taken by the Conservative Government.
Politics aside, I would like to speak about the Bill. I believe that both Bill C-18 and Bill C-19 are dangerous for all Canadians. Deregulation will be an important step to the destruction of a safe and reliable transportation network in this nation. We will be sacrificing service, safety, reliability, job security and Canadian control of our transportation industry.
During the past week both the Hon. Member for Papineau and myself have asked questions of the Government regarding near-misses and accidents which have caused the deaths of people in the United States. 1 believe that the near-misses and, perhaps, the devastating destructive death-causing crash of an airliner earlier this week were a direct result of deregulation. I think we must recognize that with deregulation, with the competition to stay in business, with cost-cutting measures and
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
the reduction of people working on maintenance, we are running the risk of creating a situation in which we will have more near-misses and more accidents causing death, not only in our skies but along our tracks and on our roads.
1 come from a riding which encompasses a great part of northern Manitoba. There are large distances between communities in my riding and people often fly in small planes from one place to another. There have been derailments and people have died as a result of truck accidents along our roads. I recognize that deregulation will create an even greater risk to people living in isolated communities, people living in the north, people who rely on a deregulated industry in which competition will be fierce and in which safety will be sacrificed.
There are already concerns in our nation with regard to the quality of air safety. At the present time there are many small companies involved in providing transportation services to remote communities, and there are a large number of accidents, many of which are caused by poor maintenance records. Many of those accidents are caused by keeping pilots in the air too long, overloading flights to realize as much profit as possible, and not adequately seating passengers. At the present time that is the history. Going into a mode of deregulation will only escalate the whole problem and the threat to the safety of Canadians.
Looking at the history of deregulation in the United States, there has been a reduction in the service to some small communities, and some that are not so small, for example, cities of 10,000, 15,000, 20,000, and 30,000. A situation is created whereby many of the companies want to do the profitable runs between Chicago-Detroit, Detroit-New York, and Seattle-New York. Many companies in Canada will want to do the runs between Toronto-Vancouver, Winnipeg-Vancouver, and Toronto-Montreal. The companies will be less interested in serving Timmins, Thompson, Prince Albert, and the other small communities. In the United States that has certainly been the experience. Companies know there are a large number of passengers on certain runs between cities with large populations, and they will either cut their services to smaller communities, or drastically reduce them.
The people in those smaller communities will suddenly discover that the flight that used to take off at 8.30 a.m. now takes off at 5 a.m. or 6 a.m., and that that is the only flight which leaves that community. In order to use the equipment for a longer period of time, air transportation becomes completely inconvenient to the people in smaller communities. I have already experienced that happening with the amalgamation of PWA and CP, and the management arrangements that are taking place with other small companies. The service is more inconvenient, the equipment is smaller, less comfortable, and obviously slower. This is already happening with the

August 20, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
threat of deregulation. When deregulation becomes a fact, more problems will be created.
The other aspect that concerns me with the general concept of deregulation is that the number of carriers in this country is decreasing. When the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry was the Minister of Transport, and this legislation was first discussed, there were a number of small, independent operators. Now PWA and CP have amalgamated and that new firm has formed management arrangements with other carriers. Air Canada has also made similar arrangements with other small carriers.
Over the last four years, instead of having competition there has been a drastic reduction in the number of carriers and independent operators. Two weeks ago, CA1, the amalgamation of CP and PWA, bought out 45 per cent of Calm Air International Ltd., a small carrier that services the people of my riding.
We are not developing a free enterprise, competitive sense in the country. The larger corporations are having complete domination. There is less service, and less competition, as a result of a Bill which is supposed to be called deregulation, and which the Government has stated will result in more competition. That simply is not happening in the area of air traffic. In the long run, I suspect that it will not happen with rail or truck transportation. In the short term, especially in the trucking industry, perhaps there will be more carriers. In the long term, we will suffer, as the Americans have, and there will be a reduction of service and in the number of carriers available to do the work.
The last area that 1 wish to deal with in the general concept of deregulation, before I deal specifically with Bill C-19, is its effect on job security. All of us in the House recognize that we are facing a pending rail strike, depending on the outcome of the conciliation talks presently taking place. The main issue is not salaries. For that matter, salaries seem to be a very minor issue in the rail talks. What is at stake is job security, and the insistence of the rail lines that they be able to contract out work that is presently done by their employees.
The reason given by CP and CN for contracting out the work, and taking away the job security of the present employees, is that they expect to be facing more and more competition in the trucking industry. Much of that trucking competition will come from American firms. In this country we are facing a strike as a direct result of the whole area of deregulation, and the legislation that will be passed in the House later today.
Employees in the rail industry may have reasonable salaries, and in the past they may have had job security. It is completely unacceptable for the employees to have their jobs threatened because the Government has a political agenda which states that we must go into deregulation and for some reason open up our trucking industry to Americans. It will not benefit Canadians to be in a situation where the owners of our trucking firms are based in Memphis. It will not help Canadians to pay taxes if the truck drivers are from Tennessee. It will not help Canadian municipalities to raise taxes if the operations are not based in their own communities. It will not help
the Province of Manitoba, which has a large trucking industry, if the trucks are based in Minneapolis. That will be the result of the legislation before us.
Perhaps as a result of the desire of the Government to come to some arrangement with the Americans on the free trade talks we will open up our doors to American firms in this transportation Bill. Yet, the Americans will not open up that same door to Canadian truckers. In the United States in the trucking industry, we cannot do what this legislation will allow Americans to do in Canada. The immigration rules and policies in the United States prevent Canadian truckers from operating in the same manner as this legislation will allow and encourage Americans, to take Canadian jobs. That is the truth. We have not heard any government Member deny that that is the truth.
As 1 have listed them, my concerns deal with the fact that we are giving up service, safety, reliability, job security, and Canadian control and ownership of the transportation industry.
As has been done with the oil industry and the mining industry, in the long run we will find that 80 per cent, 85 per cent, or 90 per cent of the transportation industry will not be Canadian, but will be owned offshore or in the United States. That is the history of the development of Canada in the case of so many of our resource industries, and our other industries.
Transportation has been one of the areas where Canadian control and ownership has remained. We have built up a proud tradition which has resulted in the employment of Canadians. We have built up a tradition which has resulted in servicing and maintenance being done in Canada. We have built up a tradition where the jobs, purchasing, and taxes have remained in this nation.
This is not so in every case. We know that CN has occasionally bought its tracks elsewhere and that CP, in terms of shipping, has quite often flown flags other than the Canadian flag. However, the bulk of the jobs and the bulk of the wealth have stayed in this country because we have had a regulated industry. With all its problems, its inconveniences, and the bureaucracy attached to it, we still managed to maintain Canadian control and to ensure that the industry operated for the benefit of Canadians.
It is interesting to note that the amendments before us at the present time are minor ones. The Government has accepted them, but basically the amendments say that we must keep some statistics on what might happen with regard to accidents in the trucking industry as a result of deregulation. That is nice and commendable and I congratulate Members of the Senate for managing to get them passed. Similar amendments were previously suggested in the House of Commons, but at that time the Government did not accept them. All they are saying is that they will keep a record and that the record will be made available to the House of Commons. They are hardly major amendments which will convince members of the New Democratic caucus to support the legislation, because its basic intent will ruin our transportation industry.
August 20, 1987

In terms of my own riding I find it upsetting that they have not said, with regard to the trucking industry, that the north should be treated differently. In the case of air transportation, we have recognized that in part of the north we really cannot expect to have a free enterprise system with 15 or 16 operators, each with one plane, no mechanics and no hangars. We recognized it for northern parts of the country, but we have not recognized it in terms of the trucking industry. We are creating a situation where there may not be adequate maintenance, garages, and trained mechanics in smaller communities. Basically we could see fly-by-night operators who come in, take the business, last for a year or two, and close.
It is interesting that that is actually happening-and it is not only a threat to people in northern Canada-in the United States with a much larger population. The number of carriers hauling less than a full load has not decreased as a result of deregulation in the United States. In fact, the reverse is true, because bankruptcies and takeovers have increased the number of general freight companies. It seems that what has happened is that with deregulation the competition is cut-throat. A business lasts for a year or two and provides a fairly cheap service, but in the long run it cannot pay its bills with the banks, do the maintenance, or provide the service necessary to maintain contracts. As a result it goes into bankruptcy and finds itself a victim of takeover.
With the American experience of less competition and worse air safety, why are we going that way? It does not make sense. We know that it will be a threat to the lives and to the safety of Canadians. At present we are being told by CP and CN that it will be a threat to the jobs of Canadians. Why are we doing it? It will not be to the advantage of Canadians. Obviously it is because of a political dogma which is unacceptable to the nation.

At the other extreme, NDP Members are vehemently opposed to any deregulation at any cost. Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
industries of Canada to be in a better position to compete world-wide.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AND CITIZENSHIP ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to once again rise in debate on Bill C-71. As I said on June 30, the Government views passage of this legislation as an essential step both in correcting historical wrongs and in reforming our laws to ensure that Canada can never be considered to be a safe haven for war criminals or those who have committed crimes against humanity. Further, the law shall apply whether those acts were committed in the past, today, or in the future.
As you know, consideration of the legislation was interrupted on June 30 by adjournment of the House, pursuant to Standing Order. Unfortunately, unanimous consent to extend the sitting to complete second reading of the Bill was not granted. I indicated at that time it would be an early priority of the Government to resume the debate when the House returned and I am pleased to be able to fulfil that commitment today.
In the interim one other significant event occurred. Following the tabling of the report of the Deschenes Commission and the Government's comprehensive response earlier this year, I indicated an additional study undertaken at the request of the commission would be made public. That study, entitled "Nazi War Criminals in Canada: The Historical Policy Setting from the 1940s to the Present" was submitted to the Deschenes Commission by Ms. Alti Rodal and, along with the other information assembled by the commission, was considered by Mr. Justice Deschenes in developing his findings and recommendations. In turn the Government provided both its detailed policy response to those findings and the recommendations and presented the legislation we are now debating here today.
Although the Rodal report contained no new information beyond that considered by the commission of inquiry, the Government believed the report contained useful contextual information and it was made public following a review by the Privy Council Office to ensure conformity with the statutory requirements of the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act.
The report speaks for itself. It traces the development of issues and policies in the past. It speaks of what is sometimes not a proud history but what is nonetheless history. It is not my intention to debate the policies and practices of past
August 20, 1987

Criminal Code
Governments. That task must fall to those who made those decisions or instituted those policies. It is up to those who are responsible to take responsibility for their acts or omissions. My task, and one from which this Government has never shied away, whether in establishing the commission of inquiry, responding to its findings, or bringing forward legislation and taking action on case files as recommended by Mr. Justice Deschenes, is to face the problem before us today. That is, to reform our laws and ensure that justice is done with respect to suspected war criminals.
Bill C-71 is a critical element in that task. It will give us the tools required to undertake prosecutions where warranted and will bring about important changes to our immigration and citizenship laws to ensure that the errors or oversights of the past are not repeated. Canadians expect their Government to undertake every step consistent with the principles of Canadian justice and the spirit of fairness and equity that is woven throughout the fabric of our nation and its institutions. Those principles are fundamental to our made in Canada policy response and they are an obligation we shall not shirk.
There is one other observation I feel compelled to make before dealing with the substantive provisions of the legislation. We must make every effort to ensure that in our zeal to bring war criminals and those who have committed crimes against humanity to justice, we do not overlook the requirements of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms and of the requirements of natural justice. I am often pressed by the media, groups and individuals, and generally by those interested in individual cases, for information with respect to the identity or whereabouts of suspected war criminals, or about the disposition of specific files turned over to the Government by the Deschenes Commission. In all good conscience, and in my capacity as Attorney General, I cannot and will not do anything that would serve to reveal information which might serve to jeopardize the right of any Canadian citizen or person resident in Canada to a fair trial. Furthermore, where there is no evidence to support prosecution or where Mr. Justice Deschenes recommended that files be closed, it is not my desire to submit persons to a form of trial by media. The requirements of Canadian justice will apply equally to all.
[Translation\
Mr. Speaker, the support which this Bill has already received, not only from Members of Parliament but also from the Canadian public, shows just how important it is.
I intend to speak mostly about the amendments proposed to the Criminal Code, but I shall also give an outline of the parts of the Bill which propose related amendments to the Immigration Act and the Citizenship Act. These amendments complement those dealing with other immigration issues which have already been introduced in this House. By proposing these amendments today, the Government is living up to its commitment to respond quickly to the Deschenes Report.

The same is true of the amendments proposed to the Citizenship Act. My colleague, the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie), recently issued a comprehensive discussion paper on citizenship, setting out in broad terms the areas to be considered for legislative review.
This is a complex matter from a legal perspective involving not only Canadian law but also principles of international law. However, I believe that the purpose of this Bill can be summarized more simply. It is that we as Canadians will not allow this country to be a haven for those persons who have committed acts or omissions which are rightly condemned throughout the civilized world.
The purpose of this Bill is to confer jurisdiction upon the courts of Canada so that the criminal law can be exercised in a manner consistent with international law and the principles of our Criminal Code. I make no apology for the somewhat intricate nature of the proposals the Government has brought before the House. They are necessary if we are to address not only those wrongs which have already occurred but also those which sadly will take place in the future.
This Bill is retrospective rather than retroactive. The acts or omissions encompassed in the definitions of war crimes and crimes against humanity have long been regarded as criminal by the community of nations. It is important to note that the military tribunal at Nuremburg reconfirmed the prior existence of these offences as have other courts since then. This Bill recognizes this fact and therefore would confer jurisdiction upon such cases.
I think it is important to stress that only offences which were known both to international law and to Canadian law at the time when such offences were committed will be brought before the courts. There will be no new offences created or applied retroactively to past acts or omissions, something which would be rightly viewed by Canadians and courts alike as repugnant to our concept of justice. Similarly, the proposed amendments to the Immigration Act and the Citizenship Act would not have retroactive application for the same reasons.
This important point is underscored by reference to the words of Mr. Justice Deschenes who said:
We are not aiming to make acts, which were deemed innocent when committed, criminal now; such would be unacceptable retroactivity. But extermination of a civilian population, for instance, was already as much criminal in 1940 as it would be today, under the laws of all so-called civilized nations. We are only trying to establish now in Canada a forum where those suspected of having committed such offences may be tried, if found in Canada.
However, I should point out to the House that international law is evolutionary and has changed over time. The definitions of war crimes and crimes against humanity reflect this. In the past, Canada has amended its laws in order to conform to its international obligations. Often these amendments have also recognized the increasing acceptance in international law of

August2(V1987
Criminal Code
the principle of according universal jurisdiction to the national courts in respect of internationally acknowledged offences.
The proposals in this Bill are made in this tradition and have been designed to respect international principles of jurisdiction with regard to any particular time period. Canada will conduct its prosecutions under the new amendments in accordance with international law.
While we must always be vigilant to ensure that the law and its application are fair, this is perhaps an instance where we must be particularly scrupulous. For this reason, the Bill contains provisions that the accused will be entitled to the full range of defences available under the laws of Canada or under international law at the time of the conduct in question and at the time of the trial. This will of course include the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In this way, it will be clear to everyone that while Canada condemns and will act against war crimes and crimes against humanity, this country will only proceed in a just and equitable fashion. 1 believe that in acting against historic evils, we are at the same time preserving historic rights.

It should be noted as well, Mr. Speaker, that the Bill contains a provision whereby a defendant can be convicted even if the offence was committed to obey orders or pursuant to the law in force at the time and in the place of its commission. I think that all members of this House and even all Canadians find it necessary to ensure that some people do not avoid prosecutions by maintaining that the act or omission they are charged with were legal in the place of their commission. In case of "war crimes" and "crimes against humanity", international law must have precedence over domestic law.

As the report of Mr. Justice Deschenes has already emphasized, the offences addressed by this Bill inevitably raise considerable emotions. The urgency the Government attaches to the enactment of this Bill recognizes the necessity of treating the problem as dispassionately, justly and expeditiously as possible in order to reassure all Canadians and to prevent intemperate individual action. I believe that this view is shared by my hon. friends opposite and I commend them for the support for this Bill which they have already shown. I am sure they will work with us to ensure that the proposals are not delayed. 1 am also most encouraged by the attitude of those groups which had legal standing before the Deschenes Commission.
The Bill also recognizes the need for prosecutions not to be undertaken lightly nor solely in response to the understandable pressure that offences of this horrible magnitude inevitably create. For this reason, proceedings will only be commenced after the personal written consent of the Attorney General or Deputy Attorney General of Canada has been given. It is proposed that the proceedings will only be conducted by the Attorney General of Canada or instructed counsel. This is in
accordance with the recommendations of Mr. Justice Deschenes.
I have already referred to the evolutionary nature of international law. The restriction on the right to prosecute also carries with it the responsibility to ensure that any action is in conformity with the treaties, rights and accords to which Canada is a party at the time such prosecution is considered. In general, this monitoring of international law is the duty of the Attorney General of Canada.
I will now turn to the amendments proposed to the Immigration Act and the Citizenship Act in support of the changes to the Criminal Code already described. I will first consider the provisions of the present Bill as they relate to the Immigration Act.
Consistent with the Government's response to the Deschenes Commission report, these changes will be prospective in nature. The single most important change to the Act is the addition to Section 19 of the Immigration Act of a new class of inadmissible persons. This new admissible class consists of persons who, there are reasonable grounds to believe, have committed a war crime or crime against humanity as these concepts are defined in the amendments to the Criminal Code.
As it is evident that no selection or assessment process, no matter how thorough, will be successful in preventing the entry of all inadmissible persons, it is necessary to provide a means for the removal from Canada of those war criminals who might be successful in slipping through the screen. This has been done through the creation of two new classes of persons against whom removal action can be taken should it come to light after they have been admitted to Canada that they have committed war crimes or that there is strong evidence suggesting that they may have committed such crimes.
The Bill also restricts appeals to the Immigration Appeal Board by persons ordered deported as war criminals to questions of law or fact. Other classes of persons having the right to appeal to the Appeal Board may do so on the basis that for humanitarian reasons, they ought to be allowed to remain in Canada. It is inappropriate that war criminals and persons who have committed crimes against humanity should enjoy this privilege.
The Immigration Act currently provides for the removal of persons to their country of citizenship, country of residence or the country from which they came to Canada. An important provision of this Bill with respect to the removal of war criminals empowers the Minister of Immigration to select any country that is willing to receive a person as the country to which he shall be deported, notwithstanding the fact that normally he would not be deportable to that country.
This provision is necessary because the country that is both willing and best able to prosecute, while at the same time offering guarantees of due process of law, may not be a
August 20, 1987

Criminal Code
country to which the person concerned would be deportable under existing Canadian law.
1 would also like to outline briefly actions being taken by the Government outside the context of this Bill to implement the recommendations of the Deschenes Commission with respect to the immigration program. The recommendation of the Deschenes Commission with respect to refugee claims by war criminals has been implemented in Bill C-55 by including in the definition of "convention refugee" the exclusion clauses contained in the United Nations convention relating to the status of refugees. These exclusion clauses include persons who have committed war crimes and crimes against humanity. Their inclusion in Bill C-55 will have the effect of preventing such persons from being found to be refugees.

In addition, the Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission is in the process of developing new administrative procedures in order to ensure that people asking for landed immigrant status will answer questions about their potential participation in war crimes or crimes against humanity. Moreover, these proceedings will mention their positive or negative answer, which could be used later as evidence.

The proposed amendments to the Citizenship Act will also be prospective in nature only. They would make involvement in a war crime or a crime against humanity a bar to the acquisition of Canadian citizenship. Section 20 would be amended in three important ways.
First, citizenship could not be acquired or resumed if the person was being investigated or charged with, on trial for, or subject to or a party to an appeal regarding war crimes or crimes against humanity unless and until that person has been fully cleared. Second, a conviction for these offences would be a permanent bar to acquisition or resumption of citizenship. Third, the onus would be placed squarely upon the applicant for citizenship to reveal any involvement in offences of this nature. Failure to do so would then render the applicant subject to prosecution and/or revocation of citizenship.
These amendments would, I believe, be a full and positive response to the concerns raised before the commission of inquiry. I am sure that the House appreciates, as I do, the swift and thorough efforts of my ministerial colleagues and their departments in addressing these related issues.
In order to avoid delay, the Government has already begun to act upon the recommendations of the commission of inquiry headed by Mr. Justice Deschenes. As he states in his report, this will require another monumental effort. Mr. Speaker, I believe that this work should proceed as soon as possible with the benefit and blessing of this House.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE, IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AND CITIZENSHIP ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we often say in this House that we are very pleased to have the opportunity to take part in a debate.

We often say what a pleasure it is to be able to participate in debate. In my case in respect to this Bill that would be an understatement. A large preoccupation of my life has been the events of World War II, in particular the holocaust, and the fact that our country, without intending it in a general sense, did become a place where a certain number of war criminals found safe haven. I think that by and large Canadians are appalled with this situation. It reflects badly on those, some in high places, who, over the decades, have been responsible for their arrival and their continued presence in our country.
It is difficult to characterize Canada as a just society or civilized place without a strong policy to bring to justice those who have committed crimes which can be characterized as war crimes or as crimes against humanity. Yet they are here. The royal commission appointed by the Government, under the exceptionally competent leadership of Mr. Justice Deschenes, presented a report with a blueprint for action. I want to acknowledge that the Government has adopted an important part of the blueprint for action, albeit not all of it. I would have liked to have seen all of it implemented, but an important part of it was implemented.
I am in the awkward situation of wanting to speak on this reading of the Bill but wanting also to see the Bill go forward quickly. Our House Leader made an offer to the Government on behalf of the Official Opposition. That offer was that we were prepared to give the Bill all three readings today, or earlier than today. We would have been prepared to have the Bill go to Committee of the Whole rather than to a regular legislative committee.
All of our willingness to expedite the passage of this Bill relates to two fundamental points. First, although the Bill can bear some improvement, we are satisfied that it will achieve the good purpose of providing for the prosecution of some war criminals. That is one reason why we support the swift passage of this Bill.
More important, however, is the fact that we are dealing with a problem which is rapidly becoming history. We are dealing with crimes committed by a small number of individuals in Canada who are aging and will be the subject of prosecution under this Bill and against whom evidence will be brought, pursuant to this Bill, by holocaust survivors who are also aging.
It is, therefore, very important that we move swiftly. While the Government has expressed a commitment, provided a royal commission, and brought forward legislation, I only say that I wish it had been done more quickly. I wish it had been done by past Governments, including the Government of which I was a part. However, I cannot refrain from commenting on the fact that if this is to be effective it must be done as quickly as possible. For that reason we supported moving through all of the stages quickly and getting on with the job in the time left on the biological clock for action against the war criminals in Canada.

August 20, 1987
Criminal Code
We will, therefore, uphold the agreement that we made to have the Bill referred to a legislative committee by five o'clock today. I hope that when the Bill is considered by a committee some amendments can be considered, not in the spirit of wanting to slow the Bill down but in the spirit of wanting to be certain that the Bill is more effective.
For example, I would like to be certain that the Bill will apply to all war criminals. While there is no doubt that the main genesis of the Bill is the holocaust which took place during World War II, there are other victims of war crimes and crimes against humanity who are living in our country. World War II was not the only war in which terrible atrocities were committed. Atrocities have been committed outside of war, against victims who have found haven in our country.
When a war criminal or a criminal who has committed a crime against humanity is living here, whether he or she comes from Europe, Asia, South America, Central America, Africa, or wherever, I want to be sure that this amendment to the Criminal Code will be available for the prosecution of that individual. Justice requires certainly no less.
I want to argue, and will do so in the legislative committee, that any individual within Canada who has committed a war crime ought to be amenable to being charged under the Bill, whether he or she has become a citizen, a landed immigrant, whether they are here on a more casual basis, such as on a work permit or as a visitor, or just passing through.
If international intelligence puts us in a position to lay a charge against someone who is in our country waiting to change planes, I think this legislation should be amenable to being used for that purpose.
Finally, in spite of the fact that Mr. Justice Deschenes recommended it, I do not think we should give a monopoly to the federal Attorney General when activating this legislation. I have great confidence in the present incumbent and I am certain he will do his duty under this legislation. I am looking forward to seeing that he does. However, I think provincial Attorneys General across the country have the competence also to bring charges under the Criminal Code. They understand the rules of evidence and deal with many matters that involve international and foreign evidence. I believe provincial Attorneys General ought also to have the door open to them to lay charges and bring forward prosecutions when they feel that it is advisable to do so, perhaps even where the Attorney General of Canada may not feel that a prosecution should be brought, in a particular case.
I want to indicate that this is only a stage and that simply passing second reading and referring this Bill to committee in no way assures that it will be passed and the Government will do the investigations and the Attorney General of Canada will lay the charges. I think the commitment that the Government has made requires it to follow through and do all those things I just mentioned.
Let me say that I am not questioning the good faith of my friend. I am only indicating that if he and his Party want the recognition and the thanks that would come from having and implementing an effective war criminals policy, it must follow through. It cannot just refer it to a committee where it will languish in a rerun of the Deschenes Committee, accepting as witnesses everyone who wants to come. In that respect, I think those who want action and wish to tell the committee that they want action will be doing themselves a disservice by seeking to appear before the committee. I hope we will be very disciplined when this Bill goes to committee, to see that we can move within a time frame I have described and have action and results.
I commend the Minister, as I commended the other steps that the Government has taken in the evolution of a war crimes policy. However, each step in itself will mean nothing if we do not proceed and reach the point where something can actually be done.
There has been talk about this issue for a long time. When we were in Government, we were able to move in a limited area. We attempted to produce extraditions and we managed to accomplish one. Certainly one was not the limit of my ambition in that area. I hoped we would be able to produce more, which I believe will be possible under this legislation.
Therefore, I want to give my support and encouragement, and that of the Official Opposition, at this stage. But let us not take too much satisfaction from reaching one stage. It is important to reach the stage where war criminals are being brought to justice.
While one was brought to justice in the former administration and more might have been brought to justice, at this stage let us at least get to one, and then more.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief because I believe all Members of the House recognize the urgency of this legislation. Indeed, as I indicated earlier, we are and have been prepared to facilitate the passage of this legislation through the House in all stages today.
I want to acknowledge the importance of the decision taken by the Government to establish the Deschenes Commission. Clearly, in the face of some 40 years of inaction, this decision was an important one. It sent out a signal that Canada at last was prepared to take seriously our responsibility to bring to justice those who were responsible for these terrible crimes against humanity.
I want to commend the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Simon Wiesenthal Centre, B'nai Brith, the Canadian Holocaust Remembrance Association and others for their tireless dedication over many years in urging Governments to take action.
As we know, it was only in 1982 that action was finally taken. I want to acknowledge the work done by the Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) within his Government in
August 20, 1987

attempting to persuade his colleagues in Cabinet to take action. Unfortunately, he was unsuccessful.
The former Minister of Justice, Mr. Chretien, stated: "I don't think we should start prosecutions in Canada for crimes committed in European countries 35 years ago". That slammed the door on any further action. I am very pleased that the Government recognized that that response was inadequate and that action had to be taken.
We know that Canada's record, both before World World II and following World World II was quite appalling. Irwin Cotier quite rightly called it the "bureaucratization of horror".
This record was eloquently documented in the report of Alti Rodal which was referred to by the Minister. In Nazi War Criminals in Canada she set out very clearly the fact that a strong anti-semitism underlay many of the actions of the Government at that time.
As Irving Abella said: "None is too many, was the underlying philosophy of those Governments". Today, surely we must recognize that our responsibility must be that one is too many when it comes to the presence of alleged war criminals in Canada.
We are not speaking in abstract terms. I think it is important to underline that we are dealing with human beings who are responsible for terrible atrocities. I recently had an opportunity to visit Ukraine where I viewed official archives, met with officials, and heard personally from men and women in Lav'in who had witnessed these terrible crimes against humanity.
There is the man with tears in his eyes who, at the age of eight, saw the village in which he had been sheltered as a young Jew be burned to the ground, subsequently returning to see the horrors of that event. There is the story of the destruction of the village of Huta Pieniacka. There is the deeply moving tale of the woman who witnessed her father being murdered in front of her eyes. We have an obligation in Canada to bring to justice those responsible for these war crimes and, indeed, all other war crimes. This legislation is an important step in achieving that objective.
The Deschenes Commission recommended other steps as well. Instead of dismissing them as the Government has done, I believe we should have seriously examined those alternatives. Apparently this Bill will go to a legislative committee where we will be proposing amendments in a number of important areas.
Let me close by quoting the words of the president of the Canadian Jewish Congress, Dorothy Reitman, who said: "The presence of Nazi war criminals in Canada has been an affront to the Canadian conscience, a moral stain, a betrayal of everything that people died for and Canadians fought for. The report of the Deschenes Commission would help to remove the stain, to redeem the victims, to right the wrong and to restore faith in the rule of law".
Soil Erosion
We have waited far too long. Let us finally move as a nation to right this historic wrong.
As I indicated earlier, I wish to seek unanimous consent of the House in order that we might proceed through all stages of this legislation today. We are prepared to proceed in this manner, given the urgency of the legislation. I would seek the unanimous consent of the House to proceed through all stages of the legislation today, through Committee of the Whole and third reading.
