speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, June 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Caccia that, in the opinion of this House,

August 20, 1987
Soil Erosion
the Government should consider the advisability of introducing a coherent, comprehensive policy and plan of action to respond to the threat of soil erosion posed to Canada's agricultural land, as described in "Soil at Risk" and "Soil Degradation in Canada".

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT SOIL EROSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to speak on this motion of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) because I have a great deal of interest in the matter of soil conservation. In my area, the riding of Perth, one of the greatest farming areas in Canada, it is of deep concern to the farmers as well.
My interest in this subject was spurred by a piece of historical fiction I read. It was about an immigrant who came, I assume legally, many years ago to the American States. As he treaded across those States, he used a test when he came to a piece of land he thought was good. He took a rod and drove it down into the ground until it came to the hard soil underneath. He measured in this way, perhaps imperfectly, the amount of topsoil. This gentleman was from Scandinavia and I assume he went to the area of Minnesota. Finally he found a piece of land where he could drive his rod down, I think it was something like 18 inches before he came to hard ground. He said to his family: "This is where we will stay. This is where we will farm because this is good land".
After reading this book, I read a report about the same area where the amount of topsoil left on many of the farms which had been farmed for perhaps 150 or 200 years was only something like five inches or six inches. This struck a bell with me. In my riding, many of our farms have only that amount of topsoil. If farmers plough deeper than six inches they turn up clay. There is very little reserve left in many of these areas.
In Ontario, which grows intensive crops of corn, they say that if you grow a 100-bushel crop of corn, you lose 100 bushels of topsoil off that land. I know that is not totally true because some land is flat and the topsoil does not run away. Some areas are protected by trees, and some areas have a lot of hills where much more topsoil runs away. I asked an expert what would happen if one had a piece of land with perhaps eight inches of topsoil and every year corn was grown for never ending time. How long would it take for all that topsoil to disappear leaving nothing on that farm? The answer was about 100 years. I saw then that our farmers today, who are farming in difficult times and with techniques that are pushed by economics, may be forced to expend the soil on their farms so there is nothing left for the farmers of the future.
This particularly worried me. We see corn grown on land year after year. We see bigger tractors used on that land because the soil gets more compacted. We see more chemicals being used on that land because without rotation, without the ability to put other crops in, one has to add chemicals to kill the weeds. We are seeing a destruction of trees which would stop some of the erosion because farmers have to use 100 per cent of their farm land. That is a very frightening prospect.
I am sure the farmers of Canada are aware of this problem. They may not know the solution. They may not know how to handle it, but they are aware of the problem. For economic reasons they cannot really stop some of their practices or do something else which would help their land.
Of course, we know that much of the cost of land degradation does not accrue to the farmer. It accrues to the societies living downstream, the cities that have to clean out the sewage, the water flows, the provinces which have to clean out the ends of rivers. The total cost does not accrue to the farmer. He may not even realize what the total cost is, although he does know the problem.
I am very interested in the motion of the Hon. Member, although I believe it is possible that there is a move already in process which will answer his concern, and perhaps this motion is simply unnecessary.
Because of the Senate report called "Soil at Risk", which was tabled in 1984, and indeed other reports mentioned by the Hon. Member in his discussion on June 19, this issue has become very important to any thinking environmentalist in Canada. It was on the agenda of the First Ministers' Conference in 1985 and as a result of the deliberations there, six working groups were set up. One of these dealt with the soil and water conservation problem. This particular working group was composed of federal and provincial officials who studied the problem and produced a report for agricultural Ministers in July 1986. This report provided the basis for the soil and water related recommendations that were put forward by agriculture Ministers in the national agriculture strategy. The soil and water conservation part of that strategy called for many different aspects but particularly for the establishment of a co-ordinated soil and water conservation program adapted to each province. In other words, it would not be the same in every province because each province's needs are different. How could one compare, for instance, the rolling land in southwestern Ontario with the flat prairie lands in the west. So each province would have a different need.
The program would provide awareness in education programs so that we ensure that everyone is aware of it, and improved extension and technical advisory services to help the farmer and the communities plan the use of the land because we cannot blame this totally on the farmer. It would provide for more on-site demonstrations of preservation techniques. It would also provide for additional research, improved financial support and assistance in areas such as soil survey work and infrastructure planning. That is all under just the one requirement of the program.
Other requirements are improvement of federal and provincial co-ordination mechanisms, a creation of a focal point for co-ordinating existing and new soil and water activities, the re-orientation of federal and provincial programs to meet needs, and the negotiation of federal-provincial agreements to finance and co-ordinate these programs, and the
August 20, 1987

establishment of local water and soil conservation organizations where appropriate action could be taken to facilitate the farmers' participation in local activities.
The national agriculture strategy calls for a federal-provincial partnership to be developed whereby both parties can define their ongoing work and in this light the federal Government has designated officers to work bilaterally toward a definition of the program by province. As well, Agriculture Canada has put together an inter-branch committee which is now in the process of defining a comprehensive national soil and water policy. In carrying out that task, federal representatives have already completed a round of consultations with each province in order to define the needs and to start the process of co-ordinating activities between each of these governments. As well as all of this, consultations with Environment Canada are under way. This is what is planned under the strategy.
Before I complete my remarks, I want to mention another program that is already in place but which has nothing to do with this strategy. It was developed separately. I refer to a soil and water environmental enhancement program which will be put in place in my area. Some $30 million in federal and provincial money will be designated to meet the problems of soil erosion. This is a program being carried out separately from the programs I mentioned before.
In thinking about environmental problems in terms of soil, we must remember that things we do in the soil can affect other areas, for example, water-tables and the quality of water that we have available in our cities for consumption. We have to keep in mind that we should not change programs so much as to cause other problems to rear their heads. It is my view that this federal-provincial approach to soil conservation will provide the coherent and comprehensive policy and plan of action called for by the Hon. Member for Davenport. It is for this reason that I maintain that his motion is simply an unnecessary one.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT SOIL EROSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am delighted to speak to the motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), and to express my appreciation for him having brought forward such a motion. The significance with respect to his bringing forward the motion is that he comes from a large urban area. I believe that the solution to the problem lies with our urban cousins as opposed to our farmers.
What is before us is an important motion. The Hon. Member can provide a valuable service to the country by visiting urban Canada, since he understands the ethics and mores of urban Canada. He can more appropriately change them than those of us who come from the rural parts of the country.
Soil Erosion
Speaking for the West, there is absolutely no doubt as to the description of the problem. In the high western plains we have been farming for some 50 years. The fertility of the western plains has dropped by some 50 per cent. If it goes down by another 50 per cent over the next 50 years, we could very easily have nothing but pure sand, which would lead to the very real possibility-in fact a probability-of seeing a massive desert in that area.
This is not a situation which can be taken lightly. The amount of soil lost in western Canada each spring is truly massive. I flew over all of southern Alberta this spring and even at a height of 18,000 feet we could barely see out the window of the plane when the winds were blowing strongly. It was not difficult to see that where farmers were using proper strip farming procedures there was no land blowing. However, where they were into farming 80 acres or more, the strips were wide enough that I could see a few pebbles rolling along on the western end which just grew and grew until the whole field was blowing away. As well, salinity is a very major problem on the high plains.
The motion before us asks for more government involvement. In fact, there is a government strategy in place. However, I want to argue that the real solution is not necessarily in more government involvement, although I think that will be the case in the short term. The solution is not necessarily in more regulation, although I believe that in the short term we will need to have more regulation. Nor is the solution implementing laws that would send farmers to jail for not stripping properly.
I submit that the real solution lies with our urban cousins, those of us who live in the small and larger urban areas, to pay more for farm produce. 1 say that for one reason. I believe that farmers want to save the soil. In fact, farmers more than anyone else want to save the soil if for no other reason than they want to conserve their income-generating asset. However, the situation goes beyond that.
Farmers have a unique attachment to the soil. Those of us who work with farmers every day and, indeed, those of us who come from the land ourselves, understand that. One has just to stand in a field after a harvest knowing that one has prepared the soil, seeded it and watched it grow, sprayed it for weeds and then swathed and harvested it. Often times one stands at the edge of the field only to see that the entire field has been destroyed as a result of a hail storm. That is a sick feeling that you would never want to have, Mr. Speaker.
If farmers received the proper amount of money for their produce there is no doubt, and I can assure anyone in the House, that we would not need laws. No farmer will let his land go down. But he needs to have a higher price for his produce so that he does not have to mine his land but actually farm it. That is where the solution lies.
With respect to grain, we have to get at our European and American neighbours who have placed us in a price war that is driving the price of grain far below the true cost of production.

August 20, 1987
Soil Erosion
How can we convince our urban cousins to do that? I am not sure. Until we can do that, even with low prices, farmers themselves are doing much, much more. Today, farmers are more knowledgeable than they were even 15 years ago when I was a young man coming off a farm. They simply know more now and they want to do better.
In southern Alberta we have a Drylands Salient Control Association which is doing absolutely first-class work in the Warner-Milk River country south and east of Lethbridge. The Government is moving. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Brightwell), set out the six task forces. We are operating at the political level, federally and provincially, and at the administrative level with the bureaucrats. We can all say that it is not going fast enough, and we do, and perhaps it is not. But at least it is moving ahead.
The long and short of it is that the solution lies in the pricing structure. If we were to get the prices up a bit-and it would not have to be a lot-farmers would make an investment in their soil and machinery that would stop us from having any problems.
I noticed in another document I was reading that we have clear objectives on acid rain, which gets into another dimension that affects farming, particularly the forest industry which is a type of farming, as well as the production of maple sugar. Canada's clear policy is that acid deposition in vulnerable areas must be reduced to less than 20 kilograms per hectare per year. I think my hon. friend from Davenport would agree with that. Indeed, when he was part of the Government he might have been part of the setting of that objective. But in order to do that, total Canadian sulphur dioxide emissions from the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border east must be reduced to 2.3 million tonnes per year. That would be some 50 per cent of the 1980 level. Also, the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide from the United States into eastern Canada must be reduced to about two million tonnes per year. Again, that is 50 per cent of the 1980 level.
Because I did not realize at first exactly all of the things that Canada was doing in this area, I want to set forth some of them. On May 22 Canada began discussions with the United States on a possible bilateral accord. It is the first time since 1982 that the two countries have engaged in negotiations that could lead to a lasting solution to the acid rain problem.
A concept paper tabled by Canadian officials outlined the nature and scope of a possible accord. The paper clearly stated that, to be acceptable to Canada, the accord must have definite targets and schedules for acid rain reduction. Specifically, Canadian representatives stressed that the flow of United States sulphur dioxide to Canada must be reduced to the 2 million tonnes that I referred to. This objective was again stressed at a July 28 meeting of Canadian and American officials. The federal Government believes that an effective U.S. acid rain abatement program requires action by both the U.S. administration and the Congress. To date our efforts have
been focused on the U.S. President. Increasingly, in the months ahead, we will be concentrating on American legislators while continuing to work with President Reagan and his administration on a bilateral accord.
As we have learned from our history when dealing with the huge republic to the south, it is not enough to deal with the administration. As a Parliament, we somehow have to develop and expand our parliamentary contacts. The Canada-U.S. Parliamentary Association does good work. The yearly meeting where they come up and sit with us in Canada, and where we go down and sit with them in the United States is a good program. Perhaps it should be expanded further. More and more the U.S. Congress is responding to narrow special interest groups. Less and less it is reacting and making decisions based on the national good of the entire United States. We too are faced with those pressures of narrow interest groups that develop sophisticated techniques, and powerful levers over us as Members of Parliament. It is difficult to take a Canadian view rather than the view of your own narrow self-interest group.
Whether it is on free trade or 100 other topics, we in Parliament have to develop a more refined mechanism in order that we can go to the United States and sit with members of Congress and have them see our Canadian perspective. I do not believe that they want to destroy North America any more than we do.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT SOIL EROSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in speaking to the motion introduced by my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). Having heard the previous speaker from the government side express his interest in and frequent involvement with farmers, I must say it astounds me that the Hon. Member spent most of his time talking about acid rain when he was involved in a discussion of such importance as reading the future agricultural production of Canada. I would have thought that the Hon. Member might have said that acid rain is an important issue, one that requires a great deal of work in order to give it prominence in the consciousness of Canadians and Americans, and that while it is a significant problem, an equally significant program is the problem of soil degradation in Canada. Perhaps he should have continued to give some constructive characterization of the problem, and its potential solutions. I regret that the opportunity was lost to enlighten this Parliament and the people of Canada on this significant problem.
I stand before you, Mr. Speaker, and unashamedly admit my fundamental ignorance of agriculture and farming. I am an urban dweller who should be made more conscious of the issues affecting the farming community. My own constituency barely has a farm, if any, within its boundaries.
It is consistent with the concerns of the former Minister of the Environment that he should raise this issue. There are a great many problems in the environment that will create a
August 20, 1987

problematic future for our children. There is a great deal of discussion of holes in the ozone layer, the greenhouse effect caused by excessive petroleum product combustion, carbon dioxide causing a future warming or cooling of our climate, the contamination of food and beverages, and the dumping of toxic and carcinogenic substances into our waters. We discuss the lead in the air from lead in gasoline.
There is also an awareness of the global problem of soil erosion. I think most people are aware of the desertification of parts of Africa, and the consequent famine. It is worth noting that wind erosion and the consequent wafting of dust in the air probably has a far more significant impact on climate than the production of pollution by our factories because it shades the earth from the sun.
Two years ago when exploring the constant stream of literature that crosses our desks, I came across a book entitled Soil At Risk. It was an impressive and informative document in terms of drawing my attention to, and enlivening my concern about soil erosion. At the same time it suggested a function that the Senate has well fulfilled, and that is being involved in long-term studies of the type that the immediate concerns of the House of Commons do not permit us to do.
When we consider the problem of soil degradation, we are considering a problem which is characteristically the type of issue with which the House has great difficulty. We are not talking about next year, much less today, but we are talking about a century from now. In the year 2050 we will be faced with serious problems of being able to maintain ourselves and our economy to the extent to which our survival is based upon a prosperous agricultural sector. Presently it is costing in the neighbourhood of $1.5 billion a year. As was earlier noted by my colleague, huge amounts of soil are being lost to cultivation. Some $20 to $35 per hectare is the average cost of soil degradation in this country. In immediate terms, this involves an area of something in the order of 650,000 Canadians, 10 per cent of our gross domestic product, and 20 per cent of our positive merchandise balance in trade.
This country can ill afford to lose its soil. Because of climatic and geological conditions, Canada has only 9 per cent of its vast land mass in cultivatable soil. Much of that area is taken up in other uses, for example, in cities, roads, forests, and other not unreasonable uses. Only 4.5 per cent of our land mass constitutes cultivatable soils. In addition to the degradation of our soil, if one envisions the future increase in our population, it is obvious that we are going in a dangerous direction. It was mentioned earlier that to a large extent the problems or the solution to the problem of soil degradation belongs to the cities, we urban residents. One of the significant causes of the loss of our richest, most fertile soil is the willy-nilly expansion of cities and towns into areas that were previously farmland. Year by year huge amounts are lost.
Soil Erosion
As I told you, Mr. Speaker, I am an urban dweller and therefore not tremendously knowledgeable about agriculture. However, 1 was a member of a regional conservation authority and 1 live in a county where soil erosion is quite marked. Whether it be by wind or by water, one knows immediately what are the causes simply by looking across our flat country. There are no trees, so in the area where I live we have exploited the land, purely and simply, without any attention to conservation.
The book "Soil at Risk", and the Science Council of Canada publication "Soil Degradation in Canada" are to be recommended to all to read.
I was interested in hearing the results of the federal-provincial conferences and other consultations on the issue of soil conservation. I would have to say, if indeed effective actions are being taken, that they are being kept quite well hidden from the general population. Certainly the most important thing which needs to be accomplished is to increase the awareness of Canadians of the dire threat to their survival and to the survival and self-sufficiency of the country as a result of the degradation of soil.
It results from wind and water erosion, from salinization, from acidification due to the excessive use, chiefly, of fertilizers, from compaction due in large measure from tilling practices, and from loss of organic matter.
As you have indicated by your signal to me, Mr. Speaker, I do not have much time to elaborate on all these issues, but it is clear that many of the problems result from the practices which are being used and often encouraged by other government policies, whether they be taxation policies, transportation policies, farm products transportation policies, marketing boards, or whatever.
There is no doubt that there is a significant difficulty on the part of the farmer in attempting to address the problem. There is no doubt that the urban dweller has a significant role to play. However, certainly the urban dweller will have to be made aware of the situation of our land as well as the situation of the farmer fighting increased costs and lower prices; facing a lack of adequate information on how to deal with the problem; and facing government practices which have failed to provide adequate research, adequate information, adequate advice, and a national policy which everyone knows would deal effectively with this very serious problem.
We have heard much about acid rain and much about the pollution of our waterways. This motion calls for not only increased awareness and action on this very serious problem, but it calls for that action to be co-operative and on the basis of concern on the part of farm dwellers and city dwellers as well.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN- EFFECT ON LAKES IN EASTERN CANADA-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER PRESS ECONOMIC ARGUMENTS WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN- EFFECT ON LAKES IN EASTERN CANADA-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER PRESS ECONOMIC ARGUMENTS WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in March of this year I raised in Question Period the findings by Dr. Schindler of the Freshwater Institute of Winnipeg concerning the impact of acid rain on the ecology, in particular on the life of organisms on which fish feed. In that process I raised the urgency for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to proceed with the matter of an acid rain agreement with the United States.
On that occasion the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) made reference to the agreements that were being discussed, at least, and to the bilateral discussions which were taking place. It was implied that Canada was to meet with the President of the United States with a clean conscience, having put into place a domestic program on acid rain from Manitoba to Newfoundland.
Today I should like to put very briefly to the Parliamentary Secretary the following chronology, in the hope that he can answer the questions I have for him flowing from the chronology and the intervention last March.
In March, 1984 the Government of Canada sought and obtained the agreement of the provinces to introduce a program which, by 1994, would implement a 50 per cent reduction in pollution emissions by producers of electricity and non-ferrous metals.
In March, 1985, the present Government confirmed that agreement and announced a detailed program.
By April, 1987, to make it short, several provinces signed that particular agreement with Ottawa, namely, Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, Newfoundland, and Prince Edward Island. We still had two provinces missing, namely, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, both of which want some funds for research or even for electric generating plants.
After enormous pressures from the committee on acid rain we finally managed to get the Premier of New Brunswick to appear before the committee on April 2. He appeared and made an announcement that he was ready to introduce a plan for New Brunswick and to sign this agreement with Ottawa. The media were there. A lot of publicity was given to that committee meeting, and Mr. Hatfield disappeared. We have not heard from him since April 2, which was just on the eve of the meeting that took place in Ottawa between the Prime Minister and President Reagan.
It was certainly well timed to convey the impression that Canada was moving, but we have not heard since from the Province of New Brunswick on the commitment it made at that time, through its Premier, that it would sign an agreement with Ottawa.
We also have another province which has not signed yet, that is, Nova Scotia. Here again that province has been dragging its feet to come through with the commitment and promise it made back in 1984 to cut its pollution in a manner which, quite frankly, is rather modest and not substantial.
Nevertheless, we have two provinces with Conservative Governments, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, that have not come through with the promise and commitment they made twice, once in 1984 and again in 1985. At the same time we see two provinces run by Liberal Governments, Quebec and Ontario, that have come through on their promises by signing an agreement. I begin to wonder whether it is perhaps Tory ideology which is impeding action by the Premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in coming through on a promise made some time ago. I cannot find any other explanation.
As I mentioned, the Premier of New Brunswick made a very clear and explicit commitment before our committee. We have not heard any word from the Premier of Nova Scotia despite letters from the chairman of the acid rain committee. Therefore, I am taking this opportunity to bring the matter to the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary. I am sure he is well briefed, and he is well known for his competence and thoroughness. I am also sure he will give us a very comprehensive reply.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN- EFFECT ON LAKES IN EASTERN CANADA-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER PRESS ECONOMIC ARGUMENTS WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government established clear objectives on the acid rain issue. To protect the Canadian environment from damage due to acidification, acid deposition in all vulnerable areas must be reduced to less than 20 kilograms per hectare per year. Achieving this objective requires that total Canadian sulphur dioxide emissions from the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border eastward be reduced to 2.3 million tonnes per year. You will know that is 50 per cent of the 1980 level. As well, the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide from the U.S. into eastern Canada must be reduced to about 2 million tonnes per year. Again, that is 50 per cent of the 1980 level.
August 20, 1987

The federal Government and the provinces are implementing a program to achieve the required emission reductions by 1994 at the latest. More than 90 per cent of the reductions required are in regulatory or program form and have been ratified in federal-provincial agreements.
The federal Government is unequivocably committed to securing an accord with the U.S. that specifies targets and schedules to reduce transboundary acid rain to the level necessary to avoid environmental damage. The Canadian objective is to have the flow of U.S. sulphur dioxide emissions into Canada reduced from 4 million tonnes to 2 million tonnes by 1994, paralleling the Canadian acid rain abatement program.
On May 22 Canada began discussions with the U.S. on a possible bilateral accord. This is the first time since 1982 that the two countries have engaged in negotiations that could lead to a lasting solution to the acid rain problem. A concept paper tabled by Canadian officials outlined the nature and scope of a possible accord.
The paper clearly stated that to be acceptable to Canada the accord must have definite targets and schedules for acid rain reduction. My friend opposite will remember that phrase because that is what he fought for when he was the Minister. Specifically, Canadian representatives stress that the flow of U.S. sulphur dioxide to Canada must be reduced to 2 million tonnes by 1994. This objective was stressed again at a July 28 meeting of Canadian and American officials.
The federal Government believes an effective U.S. acid rain abatement program requires action by both the U.S. administration and Congress. To date our efforts have focused on the U.S. President. Increasingly, in the months ahead, we will be concentrating on American legislators, while continuing to work with President Reagan and his administration on a bilateral accord.
This fall promises to be an important period for our dealings with the U.S. administration and the work of Congress. Canadians can be assured that the federal Government will continue to place a high priority on securing U.S. emission reduction targets and schedules. Our objectives and our determination could not be clearer.

subtopic: NATIONAL PAROLE BOARD-REQUEST FOR CHANGES TO PAROLE SYSTEM
NATIONAL PAROLE BOARD-REQUEST FOR CHANGES TO PAROLE SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you may recall that just about a month ago the National Parole Board granted an unescorted day pass to a man by the name of Real Chartrand. As you know, he was convicted of first degree murder and sentenced to die in 1972. This was for the murder of a police officer in Ste. Therese, Quebec. That murder occurred after a chase following a bank hold-up. While awaiting the carrying out of that sentence, in 1976 the
Adjournment Debate
Parliament of Canada repealed capital punishment. As a result, his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. He was to serve some 25 years in prison, but at the same time an amendment to the Criminal Code was passed which provided that someone convicted of first degree murder could, after just 15 years, apply to a jury and have it decide whether he or she should be eligible for parole at the end of 15 years.
Mr. Chartrand is the first person to have the opportunity to take advantage of that change. Just a month ago, after applying to a jury in the same community where he shot and killed the police officer and where he was convicted of first degree murder, the jury decided he was entitled to go to the NPB and ask for a parole after only 15 years. As you know, he did that and was given the right to unescorted day passes.
All that occurred just a few days after this House had debated the issue of capital punishment and voted on that issue in the early morning of June 30. Coming so quickly after the return of capital punishment was defeated in this House it came as a shock to many Canadians. They felt that not only was a decision made on June 30 to not increase the penalty for murder, but in fact a few days later, on July 9, there was a decision in effect by the NPB to reduce the penalty for first degree murder.
You may recall as well that in April of this year a national poll was conducted. It found that at least 62 per cent of Canadians felt that the parole system was too easy. It was too easy for people to get out on parole. Some 82 per cent of Canadians were against the idea of a week-end pass for criminals convicted of serious crimes. Only 2 per cent felt our parole system was too harsh. Only 33 per cent felt it was just right.
It is interesting and perhaps even significant to find that in the Chartrand case one of those who felt he should have received parole after 15 years was the father of the police officer murdered by Mr. Chartrand in 1972. As you will recall, he was in fact the Chief of Police of Ste. Therese at the time that incident occurred. Following the decision by the NPB to release Chartrand, the father of the slain police officer, Mr. Labelle, now retired, said that if Chartrand has rehabilitated himself, why not let him out? He said that if he had made an effort to change, give him a chance.
Mr. Labelle obviously stands with that 36 per cent of Canadians who feel that either the parole system in Canada is all right as it is or perhaps that it is even too harsh. Obviously he does not stand with the 62 per cent of Canadians who feel that there is something wrong with the parole system, it is too lenient, it should be changed and it should be changed very quickly.

August 20, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Why is it that some 62 per cent of Canadians do not have confidence in our parole system? I think the Chartrand case is perhaps a good example of what concerns Canadians about our parole system. Someone who was quite clearly convicted of the first-degree murder of a police officer was released on day passes after just 15 years. Is that in fact a proper penalty for the deliberate first-degree murder of a police officer who was in the line of duty?
It seems to me that another reason for this is the whole question the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) raised not too long ago when he said that Canadians have lost confidence in our criminal justice system. He said that the reason we have lost confidence is that the media has been sensationalizing all of these cases. It may be that that is the answer but I personally do not really think so and I know that 62 per cent of Canadians are with me. I think they feel that there is definitely something wrong with and something that has to be changed about our parole system. Having defeated the principle of capital punishment again in June of this year, they feel that Parliament now has a duty and an obligation to see that changes are made to the parole system, changes which would restore the public's confidence in that system.
In my view, we need a parole system that not only works but seems to work as far as the public is concerned. We need an entire criminal justice system that not only works but seems to work as far as the public is concerned. I hope that tonight, the Parliamentary Secretary will tell us that the Government will be unveiling such a system, a system that will restore the confidence of that 62 per cent of Canadians who just do not have any confidence at all in the present parole system. speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: NATIONAL PAROLE BOARD-REQUEST FOR CHANGES TO PAROLE SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to read, if I may, the mandate of the National Parole Board: "The National Parole Board, as part of the criminal justice system, makes independent, quality conditional release decisions and clemency recommendations. The Board, by facilitating the timely reintegration of offenders as law-abiding citizens, contributes to the protection of society."
What I have just quoted, Mr. Speaker, clearly expresses the NPB's purpose and guides the NPB's day-to-day activities. The statement is the starting point for the renewal under way within the NPB, a renewal initiated last year by the Solicitor General, Mr. Kelleher.
The Minister did not await survey results to decide to take action: for some time, in close co-operation with the chairman
of the Board, he had been analysing what changes should be made and how best to familiarize Canadians with the activities and nature of the National Parole Board.
I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, a few important changes that have already been made: the attention focussed on victims, who may now express their views to the Board in the course of its deliberations and reviews; the guarantee to victims that their testimony will be a factor in decisions on the release of offenders; the NPB's organizational review, the purpose of which was to ensure the Board's greater effectiveness as well as improvements in training, techniques and information for board members; the joint efforts of the NPB and the Correctional Service to enhance their respective contributions to the protection of society while reducing the need to build new prisons; the measures taken by the two agencies to make the transition from a prison setting to life in the community easier for the inmates; the establishment of uniform release standards, now on the verge of publication, to replace by the end of 1987 the current criteria which are too vague and general; the implementation by the Minister and the chairman of strict criteria for the selection of board members, thereby ensuring a very high level of competence.
In the end, Mr. Speaker, one reason why 62 per cent of Canadians have mixed feelings about the system may well be because the system is poorly understood. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) is perfectly aware of that stumbling-block, and that is why he has requested that the workings of the system be exposed to public scrutiny, so that everyone can see and understand how the Board reaches its decisions. In so doing, the NPB will demonstrate to Parliament, to the Government, to other agencies in the criminal justice system and to Canadians in general how the National Parole Board contributes to the protection of society.
As we have seen, Mr. Speaker, the Board is going through a period of change. The Hon. Member will, I am sure, join me in applauding what has been done so far. I am convinced, as well, that the NPB's new direction and new spirit will not only lead to greater security for Canadians but will also contribute substantially to assuaging the fear of crime, which affects the quality of life of so many people.
